abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The European Commission asked EFSA to provide support in the framework of Article 43 of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 for the preparation of the EU position for 54th Session of the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues (CCPR). In the current report, EFSA provided comments and recommendations on the Codex maximum residue level (MRL) proposals derived by the Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR) that will be discussed in the upcoming CCPR meeting. The current report should serve as the basis for deriving the EU position for the CCPR meeting.

sec.title: Summary
sec.p: For the preparation of the 54th Session of the CCPR (meeting), the European Commission asked EFSA to provide comments on the individual active substances assessed in the 2022 JMPR, in particular on the recommended toxicological reference values and the proposed maximum residue levels (MRLs) at step 3 and 6 of the Codex procedure.

In 2022, JMPR evaluated 34 active substances for their toxicological profiles and/or the residue behaviour: three of them were assessed in the framework of the periodic review (diazinon, methidathion and quintozene), nine active substances were assessed for the first time by JMPR (benzpyrimoxan, broflanilide, fluazaindolizine, fluindapyr, inpyrfluxam, isoflucypram, mefentrifluconazole, pyridate and tetraniliprole); the remaining a.s. were assessed in view of setting new CXLs for new uses (afidopyropen, azoxystrobin, benzovindiflupyr, bifenthrin, chlorantraniliprole, chlormequat, difenoconazole, dimethoate/omethoate, emamectin benzoate, famoxadone, fenazaquin, fludioxonil, flupyradifurone, flutriafol, indoxacarb, mancozeb (dithiocarbamates), mandipropamid, metalaxyl, quinclorac, spiromesifen, sulfoxaflor and triflumuron). For additional two active substances, JMPR replied to specific concerns raised by the delegations, which were submitted by means of concern forms (chlorothalonil and terbufos).

The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assessed the Codex MRL proposals as requested in the Terms of Reference and performed dietary risk assessments to support risk managers to derive a position for the upcoming CCPR meeting.

In addition, EFSA commented on the topics presented in the JMPR report in the chapter ‘General considerations’ and provided comments on the follow‐up assessments of JMPR on pesticides for which specific concerns on the toxicological or residue assessments were raised in the previous CCPR meetings.

It is highlighted that the EFSA comments were derived on the basis of the information provided in the JMPR reports. Since EFSA does not have access to the original studies and more detailed information on the JMPR evaluations, the EFSA comments are restricted to the specific questions specified in the Terms of Reference and the concise information provided in the JMPR report (2022). Hence, the comments on Codex MRL proposals reported in this report might have to be reconsidered in a more detailed assessment when needed. The comments presented in this report have to be seen in the context of the currently applicable guidance documents and the MRL legislation applicable at the time of commenting.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In accordance with Articles 5(3) and 13(e) of the European Union (EU) General Food Law (Regulation (EC) No 178/2002) 1 Codex maximum residue limits (CXLs) established by Codex Alimentarius Commission are international standards that have to be taken into consideration in the development EU standards for pesticide residues in food, to promote consistency between such international and EU technical standards while ensuring that the high level of protection adopted in the EU is maintained.

Codex MRL proposals are derived by the Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR), the scientific body responsible for the assessment of data provided by parties requesting the establishment of CXLs. The most recent JMPR evaluations for Codex MRL proposals are summarised in the JMPR Report 2022. In total, JMPR assessed 34 active substances: three of them were assessed in the framework of the periodic review, nine active substances were assessed for the first time by JMPR; the remaining a.s. were assessed in view of setting new CXLs for new uses. For additional two active substances (chlorothalonil and terbufos), JMPR replied to specific concerns raised by the delegations, which were submitted by means of concern forms. The Codex MRL proposals and the other recommendations of JMPR will be presented in the next CCPR meeting for discussion and advancement in line with the Codex procedures.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: On 8 February 2023, the European Commission requested EFSA to give advice and comments on the recommendations of the 2022 Joint FAO/WHO Meeting on Pesticides Residues (JMPR) and on the proposed Codex MRLs in order to support the Commission in its preparation of the EU coordinated positions for the 54th session of the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues (CCPR54) in 2023. This should cover the substances evaluated in the JMPR report 2022 and, where appropriate, other proposed Codex MRLs that were retained in the step procedure in previous years and may have not been covered by the JMPR report 2022 but by earlier JMPR reports.

Additionally, the European Commission requested EFSA to give its comments to the general chapters of the JMPR report 2022, where relevant for risk assessment, as well as comments on the other relevant documents for discussion in the CCPR54, e.g. as regards the proposed crop groupings and the JMPR priority list.

Lastly, the EU had introduced reservations on the draft CXLs that were proposed for pyrasulfotole, pyraziflumid, and spiropidion at CCPR53 and that have in the meantime be adopted by the Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC). The reason for the EU reservation was the lack of available toxicological data at EU level, pending the outcome of the review of the JMPR monograph which was not yet available at the time of CCPR53. Tetraniliprole was also discussed at CCPR53, even if draft CLXs were not proposed for that substance, and toxicological data about this substance, that are missing at EU level, are also present in the JMPR monograph. As soon as the monograph will be available, those CXLs should be assessed by EFSA to enable the EU to have a final view and reconsider its position.

For reasons of transparency and traceability, EFSA has created separate questions for each of the active substances covered by the mandate with the following reference numbers and subjects:

The draft scientific report of EFSA was submitted for commenting to the EU Member State experts and European Commission on 21 April 2023. All the comments received were addressed either directly in the final EFSA scientific report or though discussion during the Council Working Party meetings for the preparation of the 54th Session of the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues. The Member States consultation report (EFSA, 2023g) is a supporting document to this report, which is made publicly available. Furthermore, the exposure calculations for all crops reported in the framework of this review were performed using the EFSA Pesticide Residues Intake Model (PRIMo). A screenshot of the report sheet of the PRIMo is presented in Appendix A.

sec.title: Terms of Reference
sec.p: The requested comments to the general chapters of the JMPR 2022 report, where relevant for risk assessment, as well as comments on the other relevant documents for discussion in CCPR54 can be provided as contributions to the EU coordinated positions when these are discussed with the Member States and do not need to be covered by a scientific report.
(Terms of reference as provided by the European Commission in the Mandate of 8 February 2023)
EFSA agreed with the European Commission to respond to this request with two scientific reports.

The EFSA scientific report addressing point 1 to 3 of the Terms of Reference (ToR) was intended to be delivered by end of March 2023. However, since the JMPR report 2022 which is the basis for the assessment was published late (15 March 2023) it was agreed that the deadline for preparing the draft report was extended to 20 April 2023.

The requested recommendations point 4 and 5 (assessment of fall‐back MRLs for withdrawn CXLs and assessment of CXLs for pyrasulfotole, pyraziflumid, spiropidion, and tetraniliprole) will be presented in form of a separate report, which should be published not later than 31 January 2024.

On 21 April 2023, EFSA submitted the draft report covering the comments on the substances covered by the JMPR meeting to Member States and the European Commission for commenting. A second draft report addressing the Member State comments was completed on 19 May 2023; this document was then further discussed in the Council Working Parties held on 24 May 2023 and on 9 June 2023. The comments provided by Member States during the commenting period were addressed either directly in the final EFSA scientific report or through discussion during the Council Working Party meetings for the preparation of the 54th Session of the CCPR.

sec.title: Assessment
sec.p: In Section 3 of the report, EFSA provided comments on the discussion points presented in the JMPR report under ‘General Considerations’.
In chapters 4 of the report, EFSA assessed the responses provided by JMPR on specific concerns raised by the CCPR, requesting a re‐evaluation by JMPR.

Section 5 of the current report presents the assessments in response to point 1 to 3 of the ToR. Background information on the active substances assessed by JMPR (point 1 of the ToR) was retrieved from the database on pesticides. 2 The EFSA data management system and in‐house databases on previous EFSA assessments were used as sources of information to prepare the compilation on previous EFSA assessments. 3

In order to address the second point of the Terms of Reference on the toxicological reference values, EFSA compared the assessments performed by JMPR with the assessments performed at EU level in the framework of the peer review under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 4 or in other relevant EU assessments (e.g. MRL applications). The following sources of information were used: EFSA conclusions available for the active substances under consideration, Review Reports prepared by the European Commission, Draft Assessment Reports (DARs), Renewal Assessment Reports (RARs) prepared by the Rapporteur Member States, EFSA reasoned opinions and other sources of information if available.
For deriving the comments on the third point in the Terms of Reference (comments on the Codex MRL proposals), EFSA used the following approach to address point 3 (a) to 3 (f):

Ad 3(a): EFSA compared the enforcement residue definition derived by JMPR with the residue definition established in the EU legislation (Regulation (EC) No 396/2005) 5 or the legislation under preparation. The EU residue definitions for risk assessment were retrieved from the EFSA conclusions, EFSA reasoned opinions on the MRL review under Article 12 of Regulation 396/2005 and the reports prepared by the European Commission in the framework of the peer review of active substances or Member State evaluations in DARs. In cases where these documents are not available, the reports prepared by the European Commission in the framework of the peer review of active substances or Member State evaluations in DARs were used as source of information.

Ad 3(b): EFSA checked information reported on the analytical methods that could be used for MRL enforcement for the commodities for which Codex MRL proposals were derived by 2022 JMPR. The sources of information were the most recent JMPR report, but for a.s. that were already assessed in previous years, EFSA looked up information in previous JMPR reports. As the level of detail on validation data is rather limited in the JMPR report, EFSA could not verify in detail whether the methods were sufficiently validated.

Ad 3(c): The comparison of the EU MRLs and the Codex MRL proposals is presented in tabular form. Codex MRL proposals that are higher than the existing EU MRLs are printed in bold. In line with the presentation of MRLs in the EU legislation, limit of quantification (LOQ) MRLs are labelled with an asterisk (‘*’) after the value. The comparison of Codex MRL proposals with existing EU MRLs is performed for commodities listed in Part A of the EU food classification (Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005), but not for products that are listed in Part B.

Ad 3(d): For assessing whether the draft Codex MRL proposals for plant products are sufficiently supported by data, EFSA focused on the availability of residue trials and metabolism studies. If the data used to derive the Codex MRL proposal were in accordance with the number of trials specified in the FAO manual (FAO, 2016) and the agreed policy of JMPR, the Codex MRL proposals are considered to be sufficiently supported by data and the MRL proposals are flagged as ‘the proposed Codex MRL is acceptable’. Details on independence of residue trials, storage stability, analytical method validation and other details, which would be assessed in detail in the framework of EU MRL applications, are not reported in the JMPR reports. Hence, comments on these aspects of the dossier are not within the scope of the current assessment.

For animal products, EFSA verified the plausibility of the Codex MRL proposals, based on the information provided in the JMPR reports on the results of dietary burden calculations and feeding studies. If the Codex MRL proposals for animal products passed the plausibility check, they are considered appropriate. A verification of the dietary burden calculation for all global regions (Europe, USA/Canada, Australia, Japan) cannot be performed in the framework of the current mandate, because comprehensive information on all authorised uses for feed commodities other than the commodities assessed by JMPR is not available to EFSA. In addition, the EU tool used for calculating the dietary burden does not comprise livestock diets from non‐EU regions.

Ad 3(e): In order to assess the overall appropriateness of Codex MRL proposals as requested in the ToR, EFSA derived a conclusion on the availability of representative residue trials compliant with the residue definitions (considering also the extrapolation and scaling rules) and verified the MRL calculations (based on the OECD calculator; OECD, 2011). In addition, relevant points for risk management consideration were reported. The Codex MRL proposals are reported as acceptable/appropriate, if no obvious deficiencies were identified based on the information presented in the JMPR reports. If serious deficiencies are noted or if the Codex MRL proposals lead to chronic and/or acute public health concerns, the Codex MRL proposals are reported as not acceptable. In case, relevant points not directly related to the scientific assessment were identified which require further risk management considerations, EFSA recommends further discussions to decide whether the Codex MRL proposals are acceptable.

Ad 3(f): For the assessment of the safety of the draft Codex MRL proposals, EFSA used the revision 3.1 of the EFSA Pesticide Residues Intake Model (PRIMo) (EFSA, 2018c, 2019k). For assessing the short‐term (acute) consumer risk, EFSA applied the standard EU methodology, including the agreed EU variability factors. For the assessment of the long‐term (chronic) consumer risk, EFSA calculated the exposure resulting from the existing EU MRLs, taking into account the most recent information on supervised trials median residues (STMRs) and including the STMR values derived by JMPR for commodities where the proposed Codex MRLs are higher than the existing EU MRLs. For active substances where the MRL review has not yet been completed, less refined calculations were performed: for commodities where the EU MRL is higher than the proposed Codex MRL, the EU MRL was used as input values for the risk assessment instead of the STMR value. The contribution of the individual crops under consideration in the CCPR meeting was calculated separately.

For pesticides where the EU and JMPR residue definitions for risk assessment are not comparable, EFSA calculated indicative risk assessment scenarios. The assumptions and uncertainties of these scenarios are described individually. The exposure assessments are usually compared with the EU toxicological reference values, unless it is specifically mentioned that the JMPR values were used. The used approaches are considered to be sufficiently conservative for a risk assessment screening.

Finally, it should be mentioned that due to the different requirements, scientific and procedural guidelines and policies used at EU level and by JMPR, the assessment of residue data sets submitted in support of an EU MRL application and Codex MRL request may result in different recommendations at EU level and by JMPR.

It is noted that comments were derived on the basis of the JMPR reports summarising the recommendations of the 2022 JMPR meeting, which was published on 15 March 2023. Due to the timelines agreed with the requestor, EFSA could not use the more detailed information presented in the JMPR evaluations which were published at a later stage to prepare the comments. EFSA also does not have access to the original studies assessed by JMPR. Thus, the conclusions reached in this report should be considered as indicative and might have to be reconsidered in a more detailed assessment, when needed.

sec.title: Comments on chapter ‘General Considerations’ of JMPR reports
Requirements for data on the impact of residues on the human intestinal microbiome
sec.p: JMPR proposes to establish a microbiome expert working group to develop guidance for discussion and adoption by JMPR. The guidance shall build on the long experiences of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) in assessing residues of veterinary drugs, in particular antibiotics, for their potential impact on the human microbiome, specifically in view of the disruption of the bacterial colonisation barrier and the increase of bacterial resistance. Since effects on the microbiome are not only expected for antibiotics, but also other chemicals, such as pesticide residues, JMPR should address this aspect in its assessments, which should not only focus on bacteria, but also other components of the intestinal microbiome, such as fungi, archaea, protozoa and viruses.

To facilitate these assessments, JECFA adopted guidance from the International Cooperation on Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Registration of Veterinary Medicinal Products, VICH GL36(R), which outlines a stepwise approach to determine if a microbiological acceptable daily intake (mADI) would be necessary. A mADI is required, if the following three conditions are fulfilled: the compounds (parent or metabolite) are microbiologically active against human intestinal microbiota and they have the potential to enter the human colon, maintaining the microbiological activity in the human colon. In addition to mADIs, JECFA also establishes microbial Acute Reference doses (mARfDs) to address acute effects of veterinary drug residues to the human microbiome.

EFSA notes that currently the assessment of microbiome(s) is not part of the regulatory requirements for plant protection products and their residues and no internationally agreed guidelines are in place in the pesticide area. EFSA concurs with JMPR considerations on the potential relevance of chemicals (including pesticides and their residues) on human and animal intestinal microbiome and reckons that further developments are needed in this area to understand the importance of the microbiome in risk assessment and identify dedicated strategies and methodologies accordingly. EFSA is working on this subject: to start building this capacity, EFSA launched a thematic grant in March 2020 to collaborate with EU Member States and to identify indications for future EU research agendas with a focus on specific needs from a risk assessment perspective.

sec.title: Non‐linear kinetics (KMD)
sec.p: EFSA agrees that more guidance on assessment and interpretation of non‐linear dispositional kinetics would be desirable. The guidance should more generally deal with the interpretation of non‐linearity in the dispositional kinetics of pesticides. EFSA notes that at EU level, hazard classification is an important element to decide on the approval of an active substance. According to ECHA – the EU agency responsible for classification and labelling – the kinetically‐derived maximum dose (KMD) approach is not suitable/not appropriate to fulfil the legislative needs for classification and labelling; instead, the maximum tolerated dose (MTD approach; with inclusion of the non‐liner kinetic only as a complementary information) would be the most appropriate methodology to derive selection of the high‐dose level for toxicological studies.
Further information on the electronic Working Group (eWG) and the progress of the activities would be desirable.

sec.title: Interpretation and follow‐up of positive results in in vitro gene mutation assays
sec.p: EFSA welcomes JMPR clarifications on the interpretation and follow‐up of positive results in in vitro gene mutation assays. JMPR outlines the testing strategies for follow‐up of positive results in in vitro gene mutation assays.

The proposed follow‐up tests are not fully in line with the EU approaches.
JMPR proposed the in vivo transgenic rodent somatic and germ cell gene mutation assays as a follow‐up in vivo test. However, the EFSA Scientific Committee considers that routine testing for genotoxicity in germ cells is not necessary (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2011).
JMPR also proposed that ‘for bacterial gene mutation caused by non‐DNA reactive gene mutagens (for instance intercalating agents likely to be detected only by tester strains such as TA 1537 used in the Ames test) the in vivo alkaline comet assay is not appropriate and the transgenic rodent somatic and germ cell gene mutation assays are the recommended test’. EFSA considers more appropriate to state that the in vivo Comet is not appropriate for substances that are not considered to induce single‐strand breaks or double‐strand breaks (SSBs or DSBs), either directly or via DNA repair intermediates, based on structural considerations and positive results in TA1537 and TA98.
As regards clastogenicity and aneugenicity endpoints, JMPR also commented that in the case of a positive in vitro chromosomal aberration assay or in vitro micronucleus assay the recommended follow‐up is the in vivo micronucleus assay. EFSA suggests adding that evidence of target tissue exposure should be demonstrated in the in vivo micronucleus assay (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2011, 2017).

sec.title: A risk‐based decision tree approach for the safety evaluation of residues of pesticides, veterinary drugs, food additives and contaminants
sec.p: EFSA welcomes the discussion to develop an approach for giving advice to risk managers on substances which are found in food, but for which the data are insufficient to perform a full risk assessment.

In EFSA's view, it is necessary to develop different approaches for approved/authorised substances and for unavoidable, naturally occurring contaminants (e.g. contamination of food with previously used substances because of their environmental persistence). According to the updated EFSA guidance (EFSA Scientific Committee, 2019), the use of the threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) approach is a pragmatic, scientifically valid methodology to assess the safety of substances of unknown toxicity found in food and the environment. However, the TTC approach should not be used for substances for which EU food/feed legislation requires the submission of toxicity data. Hence in the EU, the TTC approach is usually not applied for pesticides to waive toxicological studies defined in the legal data requirements.

In case of unavoidable contaminations in absence of sufficient data to establish health based guidance values, the use of the TTC approach may be useful to provide advice to risk managers and for this purpose a decision tree might be helpful.

EFSA noted that the decision tree is very unspecific about certain details, e.g. the methodology how to calculate the exposure, the subgroups of the population for which exposure estimations should be derived. In addition, it would be necessary to define the criteria like ‘meaningful margin of exposure’, ‘low margin of exposure’ or ‘acceptable margin of safety’ integrated in the version of the decision tree presented in the JMPR report.

sec.title: Unnecessary use of in vivo animal studies
sec.p: EFSA strongly supports the recommendations of JMPR to avoid unnecessary in vivo studies. It is highlighted that in the EU, the replacement, reduction and refinement of the use of animals for scientific studies supporting applications for pesticide approvals and MRL applications are a fundamental principle implemented in the pesticide legislation.

sec.title: Establishment of MRLs for pesticides for okra
sec.p: EFSA appreciates the comprehensive work done by JMPR to evaluate monitoring data and to analyse the normalised initial residue concentrations measured at day 0 in different fruiting vegetables in view of identification of options for setting MRLs in okra by extrapolation.

EFSA agrees with the conclusion of JMPR that monitoring data are not appropriate to find representative commodities for okra, since for monitoring data usually no information is available on the treatment history. Without information on the use patterns, a meaningful interpretation of these data is not feasible.

The available data on normalised residue trials do not provide sufficient evidence that the residue behaviour in other fruiting vegetables is comparable to okra. Hence, the data do not support option 1 and option 2 on the classification of okra in the Codex food classification; option 3 (introduction of a specific sub‐group for okra (including martynia and roselle)) seems to be the only viable option at the moment.

Acknowledging the difficulties in generating data for the minor crop of okra, it is recommended to explore if normalised residue data at day 0 in other crops show comparable residue levels with okra. If this is the case, it might be a solution to allow specifically for okra an extrapolation from another crop not belonging to the group of fruiting vegetables, provided there is sufficient evidence to conclude that the residue behaviour is comparable.

sec.title: Enhancing operational procedures of JMPR to reduce the backlog
sec.p: EFSA supports the discussion to identify opportunities for enhancing the operational procedures of the JMPR and CCPR to reduce the backlog of evaluations. EU experiences on streamlining the assessment processes might be helpful to identify steps of the process which could be improved.

sec.title: OECD update to the guidance on residue definitions
sec.p: The active involvement of JMPR experts in OECD projects should be encouraged, as JMPR experts have a lot of experiences in assessments at international level and therefore they are expected to provide valuable input to the development of OECD documents.

sec.title: Information on residues in rotational crops following use on paddy rice
sec.p: For European rice cultivation, crop rotation is not completely excluded, but is expected to take place only after several years of cultivation of rice. For EU assessments, a new guidance document on rotational crop assessment is under preparation. In a draft version of this guidance document, rice is considered as semi‐permanent crop. Hence, primary crop uses in rice would not trigger rotational crop studies. If rotational crop studies are required due to uses in other primary crops than rice, it is not recommended to conduct rotational crop studies (confined studies and higher tier studies) with rice (crop grown as rotational crop) to investigate the uptake from residues in soil. Instead, other cereal crops should be used as test crop for rotational crop studies, as rice is considered not a crop representative for other cereals.

sec.title: Common pyrazole metabolites
sec.p: The a.s. assessed by JMPR in 2022, belonging to the pyrazole class are the following: benzovindiflupyr (261), chlorantraniliprole (230), inpyrfluxam (329), isoflucypram (330) and tetraniliprole (324).

It is noted that for a number of additional a.s. containing a pyrazole structure, CXLs are in place, e.g. for fenpyroximate (193), fipronil (202), pyraclostrobin (210), isopyrazam (249), fluxapyroxad (256), sedaxane (259), bixafen (262), cyantraniliprole (263), oxathiapiproline (291) and ethiprole (304).

A more general approach for assessing common metabolites should be elaborated. At EU level, for triazole derivative metabolites (TDMs) a risk assessment approach which comprises the different sources of triazole metabolites has been elaborated. A similar approach should be established for class of pyrazole pesticides.

sec.title: Responses to specific concerns raised by the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues (CCPR)
Chlorothalonil (81)
sec.p: At CCPR52, the UK submitted a concern form stating that the degradation product R613636 identified in standard hydrolysis studies representative for sterilisation has not been sufficiently addressed in the acute and chronic exposure assessment performed for the Codex MRL proposal for cranberries.

In response to this concern form, JMPR assessed additional processing studies in barley, wheat, cabbages, common beans with pods and tomatoes. In processed products, residues of R613636 were below the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg, except in one sample of wheat germ (0.02 mg/kg). JMPR performed a conservative exposure calculation and concluded that the acute and the chronic exposure is below the Cramer class III TTC of 1.5 μg/kg bw (body weight) per day. Based on this assessment, JMPR concluded that the exposure to R613636 is not expected to be a safety concern.

EFSA does not agree with the conclusion of JMPR for the following reasons:
The processing studies are not fully representative for the existing CXLs as the residues in unprocessed cereals products used as the starting material for the processing studies residues were significantly lower (0.24 mg/kg and 0.02 mg/kg) than the CXLs for cereals (ranging from 2 to 6 mg/kg). Hence, the exposure calculations for processed products which contained residues at low levels or below the LOQ may underestimate the exposure, if cereals contain residues at the level of the Codex MRL.
Processing studies for animal products are not available. Considering that for milk, meat and other animal products CXL are established (e.g. CXL for milk 0.3 mg/kg, CXL for meat 0.2 mg/kg), and these products which are consumed after processing, are an important component of the human diet, information on the residue levels of R613636 expected in processed animal products should be provided.

It is also highlighted that in 2022, the EU identified additional concerns on metabolite R182281 (SDS‐3701) and R417888, which are still not sufficiently addressed. These additional concerns referred to the lack of an appropriate in vivo follow‐up for positive results in the mammalian gene mutation assays with both metabolites. EFSA and JMPR would agree that a Comet assay or transgenic rodent gene mutation assay are appropriate in vivo follow‐up for substances positive in the gene mutation assays (see chapter 2.3). Several in vitro gene mutation assays were available for both metabolites. The main discrepancy is that JMPR considered an overall call for in vitro mammalian gene mutation as negative (considering all studies results) whereas for EFSA, having the uncertainties over the results of in vitro mammalian gene mutation assays (inconsistent results), would consider more appropriate to follow‐up them in vivo. Therefore, according to EFSA the genotoxic potential of metabolites R182281 (SDS‐3701) and R417888 are currently inconclusive.

sec.title: Terbufos (167)
sec.p: In CCPR53, the EU expressed its concern about the outdated toxicological assessment of terbufos that has not been updated since 2003. The EU referred to a more recent Canadian notification to the Rotterdam Convention (PIC procedure), where the Canadian authorities derived an acceptable daily intake (ADI) and an acute reference dose (ARfD) which were 4 times and 10 times lower, respectively than the JMPR toxicological reference values.

In the 2022 report, JMPR briefly summarised the findings of the acute neurotoxicity study which was used to derive the ARfD by JMPR and by the Canadian authorities. While both, JMPR and Canadian assessment, derived the same no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL), the Canadian assessment applied an additional uncertainty factor due to the steep dose response. JMPR did not see the need for this extra factor of 10 and concluded that there was no evidence to review the ADI and ARfD ahead of its scheduled periodic review (terbufos is listed in table 2B 6 and in table 5 7 of the schedules and priority list prepared by the eWG on priorities).
It is noted that in the short assessment provided by JMPR, no information on the ADI difference was reported. Further clarifications should be requested from JMPR.

More importantly, it should be highlighted that the EU concerns on the outdated toxicological assessment were of general nature, not restricted to the acute neurotoxicity study, which was used to derive the ADI and ARfD for parent terbufos. The EU concerns were raised because a toxicological assessment of terbufos and metabolites expected in food is not available. Such an assessment should address the genotoxic potential of terbufos and its metabolites, but also the general toxicity for the individual components of the residue definition.
Hence, EFSA concludes that the EU concerns have not been sufficiently addressed by the information provided in the JMPR report.

In the framework of the periodic review of JMPR, the toxicological data have not been re‐evaluated, since JMPR performed a comprehensive re‐evaluation in 2016.

The ADI established by the JMPR (2016) is based on the NOAEL 0.3 mg/kg bw per day from all repeated‐dose toxicity studies and applying an uncertainty factor (UF) of 100; it is supported by human studies for which an UF of 10 was applied.

The ARfD established by the JMPR (2016) is based on the NOAEL 2.5 mg/kg bw per day (for red blood cell (RBC)) and brain AChE inhibition in acute neurotoxicity studies in rats and applying and UF of 100, this value is supported by humans studies on which an UF of 10 is applied.

General comment on the metabolism studies used to derive the residue definitions:

EFSA noted that all metabolism studies were performed with diazinon radiolabelled in the pyrimidinyl ring. There is evidence of cleavage of the ether bond. tr.td: In the EU, the previously established TRVs have been withdrawn.

td.p: EFSA (2018) (dimethoate).
Considering that omethoate showed genotoxic potential in vivo, the setting of reference values is not considered appropriate.

For omethoate, JMPR derived an ADI 2.5 times lower than the ADI set for dimethoate (i.e. ADI of 0.0004 mg/kg bw) and an ARfD 10 times lower than the ARfD set for dimethoate (i.e. ARfD of 0.002 mg/kg bw).

Genotoxicity: Positive/equivocal response in a number of in vitro tests, including
a bacterial reverse mutation assay,
sister chromatid exchange (SCE),
forward mutation assay in mammalian cells (HPRT test) and
unscheduled DNA synthesis in mammalian cells.
Positive responses were only obtained at either high or severely cytotoxic concentrations and with no clear dose‐dependency.

Omethoate gave negative responses in vivo in
the micronucleus,
SCE and
unscheduled DNA synthesis tests.

In the EU peer review, an almost complete toxicological dossier was provided for omethoate. Omethoate is a more potent AChE inhibitor than dimethoate. The metabolite presents a higher acute toxicity by the oral, dermal and inhalation routes. However, considering that omethoate showed genotoxic potential in vivo, the setting of reference values was not considered appropriate and the previously established TRV for omethoate were withdrawn.

caption.p: Comparison of Codex MRL proposals derived by JMPR with EU MRLs

td.p: cGAP: AUS, post‐harvest dip with 0.04 kg a.s./100 L, no withholding period defined.
Number of trials: 4 trials in mandarins and 6 trials in oranges. Separate results reported for dimethoate and omethoate, for whole fruit and peeled product (flesh), respectively.
Sufficiently supported by data: To be discussed

Specific comments: As mandarins are a major crop according to Codex classification, 4 mandarin trials are not sufficient to derive an MRL proposal. JMPR therefore merged the data on oranges and mandarins to have a sufficient data package. However, orange data normally cannot be used to derive MRLs for mandarins. The HR/STMR values were derived from the peeled product. It is therefore recommended to discuss whether the number of trials is sufficient to derive an MRL proposal for mandarins. The peeled samples were analysed directly after the treatment, and no residue decline data are available. It is expected that the residue concentration in the flesh/peeled product increases with time and/or the amount of the more toxic metabolite omethoate increases. Hence, the risk assessment values derived by JMPR are likely to underestimate the risk for consumers.

Conclusion: The proposed Codex MRL is not acceptable because in the EU, no TRV were derived to perform a sound risk assessment. In addition, RM are invited to discuss whether the data set is considered sufficient to derive an MRL proposal for mandarins; the merging of orange and mandarin trials is not in line with the Codex extrapolation rules.
Follow‐up action: None

caption.p: Summary of the consumer risk assessment

td.p: RA assumptions: An indicative short‐term dietary risk assessment (PRIMo rev. 3.1) was performed for the Codex MRL proposal, using the HR/STMR values derived by JMPR for acute risk assessment (considering the 10 times higher potency of omethoate compared to dimethoate).
The risk assessment was performed with the JMPR ARfD.
The calculations are indicative, because in the EU no TRV were established.

The calculations are affected by additional, non‐standard uncertainties due to the non‐adequate study design for citrus fruit and avocados which are likely to underestimate the residues and the insufficient number of residue trials for dry beans.

RA assumptions: An indicative long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1, using the STMR values derived by JMPR for chronic risk assessment (considering the 2.5 times higher potency of omethoate compared to dimethoate).
The risk assessment was performed with the JMPR ADI.
The calculations are indicative, because in the EU no TRV were established.

tr.td: Specific comments: Dietary intake was calculated for the combined adjusted residues of omethoate (taking into account the higher potency of omethoate) and dimethoate and compared to the ADI/ARfD set for dimethoate.

It is noted that in the context of the recent MRL review under Art. 12 of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 (EFSA, 2023e), EFSA proposed the following residue definitions applicable for plant and animal products:
RD enf: dithiocarbamates (dithiocarbamates determined and expressed as CS2, including maneb, mancozeb, metiram, propineb, thiram and ziram)
RD RA: (1) mancozeb (analysed as CS2 and expressed as mancozeb)
RD RA: (2) ETU
For enforcement purposes the EU and JMPR residue definitions are comparable. To express the residues of mancozeb as CS2, the molecular weight conversion factor of 1.78 is applicable.

For risk assessment purposes the residue definitions differ as the RD set by the JMPR includes metabolite ETU, which, according to the JMPR assessment, is 7.5 times more toxic than parent compound. Therefore, to express residues of ETU as mancozeb toxicity equivalents the ratio of the ADIs of mancozeb and ETU (7.5) is used by the JMPR.
In the EU, ETU is included in a separate residue definition, to be assessed against the TRV derived for ETU.

caption.p: Summary of the consumer risk assessment

td.p: EFSA derived the input values for the short‐term risk assessment from the information presented in the JMPR report. As the EU residue definition comprises only mancozeb, the highest/median CS2 result from the data set used to calculate the MRL was identified. This value was then re‐calculated to mancozeb, using the conversion factor of 1.78.

EFSA noted that for all commodities assessed by JMPR the respective risk assessment values were lower than the values used in the most recent risk assessment performed for mancozeb (EFSA, 2023e), except for longan (classified in the EU under litchies).
Hence, EFSA calculated the short‐term exposure only for this commodity, using EFSA PRIMo rev. 3.1.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ARfD.
The calculations are indicative, because specific consumption data for longan berries are not available in the EFSA PRIMo. Instead, the consumption data for litchis were used.
The exposure calculation could be further refined if appropriate data are provided on the residues in the edible part of the crop (e.g. a peeling factor for longan/litchi).

A long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1. The input values of the most recent long‐term risk assessment (EFSA, 2023e) were updated, including the STMR values derived from the JMPR report as describe in the risk assessment assumptions for the acute exposure assessment.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ADI.
The calculations are indicative, because a decision on the modification of the existing EU MRLs as proposed in the EFSA MRL review has not yet been discussed/decided.
The JMPR assessed combined residues of mancozeb and ETU using the ratio of the ADIs (7.5) to express residues in terms of mancozeb‐toxicity‐equivalents (MTE).

EFSA did not identify a short‐term consumer health risk for the crop under assessment but noted a very narrow margin of safety in the calculation performed in accordance with the internationally agreed methodology (using HR, IESTI case 1).
Litchis (longan): 98% of ARfD
It is noted that if litchis contain residues at the level of the proposed Codex MRL, the ARfD is exceeded.
No long‐term consumer health risk was identified.
The overall chronic exposure accounted for 40% of the ADI.
Litchis contribution to the overall long‐term exposure: 8.4% of the ADI.
Long‐term exposure:
Max 50% of the JMPR ADI.
Short‐term exposure:
Not relevant (JMPR did not derive an ARfD).
EFSA derived the input values for the short‐term risk assessment of ETU from the limited information presented in the JMPR report.

Similar to the approach of JMPR, EFSA assumed that in those commodities that can be consumed only after processing (i.e. cotton seed, maize, rice husked and soy beans dry) mancozeb residues are completely converted to ETU. The STMR values reported as CS2 were recalculated to mancozeb, applying the molecular weight conversion factor of 1.78. In a second step, the mancozeb residues were recalculated to ETU, applying a conversion factor of 0.38 (MW of mancozeb: 541, 1 mol of mancozeb can produce 2 mol of ETU (2 × 102.2 (MW of ETU)), ratio of ETU/mancozeb = 204.4/541 = 0.38).
For longan, the HR of mancozeb was recalculated to ETU, assuming a complete conversion in processed (canned) fruit, using the same conversion factors.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ARfD.

The calculations are indicative and affected by additional, non‐standard uncertainties, as empirical data on the expected ETU concentration in the commodities under assessment are not available. In addition, as specific consumption data for longan were not available, the calculations were performed with the consumption data of litchis. Overall, the risk assessment approach is considered conservative and could be further refined, if more information on the actual ETU residues is provided.

A long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1. The input values of the most recent long‐term risk assessment (EFSA, 2023e) were updated, including the STMR values derived from the limited information presented in the JMPR report. The STMR values for cotton seed, maize, rice husked and soya beans calculated for the acute risk assessment were used for the calculation. By analogy, the STMR for longan was calculated.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ADI.

The calculations are indicative, because a decision on the modification of the existing EU MRLs as proposed in the EFSA MRL review has not yet been discussed/decided. The calculations are also affected by additional, non‐standard uncertainties, as empirical data on the expected ETU concentration in the commodities under assessment are not available
Other sources of ETU from other dithiocarbamates were not considered in the chronic risk assessment. Therefore the results may underestimate the long‐term exposure.
The calculated short‐term exposure exceeded the ARfD for one crop under assessment.
Litchis (longan): 558% of ARfD
It is noted that if litchis contain residues at the level of the proposed Codex MRL, the ARfD is exceeded.
No long‐term consumer health risk was identified.
The overall chronic exposure accounted for 69% of the ADI.
Litchis contribution to the overall long‐term exposure: 37% of the ADI (GEMS/Food G11).

tr.th: Findings relevant for discussion of EU position

tr.td: A.s. no longer approved in the EU; the a.s. falls under cut‐off criteria. MRL review ongoing.
EU and Codex RDs for enforcement are comparable.
Analytical methods for MRL enforcement are available.

The proposed Codex MRLs are sufficiently supported by data. For rice, discussion with RM recommended to decide whether the MRL proposal derived from the subset of the residue trials (omitting the trials with residues below the LOQ) is acceptable.

td.p: No chronic intake concern was identified for mancozeb. In the acute risk assessment for mancozeb, a very narrow safety margin was identified for longan.

For ETU, a conservative indicative risk assessment was performed which lead to an exceedance of the ARfD. Further refinements might be possible, if the conservative assumptions are replaced by more realistic data derived from appropriate studies which are currently not available to EFSA.

tr.td: Further risk management discussion required to decide on the EU position.

td.p: General comment on the metabolism studies used to derive the residue definitions:

EFSA noted that all metabolism studies were performed with methidathion radiolabelled in the thiadiazol ring. There is evidence of cleavage of the thioether bond. Hence, the presence of metabolites containing the dimethyl dithio phosphorothioate moiety are likely to occur and should be investigated, in particular in view of the toxicological profile.

For risk assessment, JMPR included an additional metabolite (M8) in the residue definition for plant commodities. Based on metabolism studies, a conversion factor of 1.3 was derived to address the metabolite expected in fruit crops if the metabolite was not analysed in residue trials.
The difference of the risk assessment residue definition for animal products is of no relevance for the current assessment.

caption.p: Summary of available analytical methods

td.p: A modification to the method (method REM 181.06), with the introduction of an HPLC chiral separation step before determination, allows for the analysis of specific enantiomers (JMPR 2004).

A multi‐residue regulatory method (DFG S19) is available for metalaxyl. Method REM 181.06 (gas–liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry detection) is not a multiresidue method, but it is enantioselective and suitable as a regulatory method for metalaxyl‐M (JMPR 2004).

tr.td: Extraction with acetone and dichloromethane, clean‐up, determination with GC‐NPD
JMPR 2022 noted that very limited validation date were provided for this method used to analyse pineapple residue trials.

td.p: Common moiety methods rely on the 2,6‐dimethylaniline moiety of metalaxyl and many of its metabolites, and these methods have been used to identify metalaxyl residues in animal commodities (JMPR 2004).
The typical LOQs are 0.05 mg/kg for tissues and 0.01 mg/kg for milk.
Metabolite 8, containing the 2‐hydroxymethyl‐6‐methylaniline moiety, is apparently partially converted to 2,6‐dimethylaniline, resulting in low and variable recoveries.

caption.p: Summary of the consumer risk assessment

td.p: A short‐term dietary risk assessment (PRIMo rev. 3.1) was performed for the commodities, for which the Codex MRL proposal is higher than the existing EU MRL (i.e. pineapple. It is noted that for ginseng no EU consumption data are available; hence a risk assessment could not be performed).
CF of 1.3 for fruits derived by JMPR from metabolism studies to compensate the contribution of M8 were also used in the calculations.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ARfD (same as the one derived by JMPR).
The calculations are likely to overestimate the exposure, because the RD‐RA for plants derived by JMPR is wider than the RD proposed at the EU level.

A long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1. The input values of the most recent long‐term risk assessment (EFSA, 2023f) were updated, including the STMR values derived by JMPR for the crops for which the proposed Codex MRL is higher than the EU MRL (i.e. pineapple and ginseng).

The presented scenario the following approach was used: for crops for which no confirmatory data were provided, the lowering of the existing MRL to the LOQ or an alternative fall‐back MRL were anticipated (e.g. to an MRL reflecting a less critical EU use or to a Codex MRL). Codex MRLs adopted in CAC 2022 were also included, provided the EU did not express a reservation and the EU MRL is lower than the new CXL.
Only for pineapple the CF derived by JMPR from metabolism studies (CF of 1.3 for fruits) was used in the calculations to compensate the contribution of M8.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ADI (same as the one derived by JMPR).
The calculations are likely to overestimate the exposure, because the RD‐RA for plants derived by JMPR is wider than the RD proposed at the EU level.
No consumption data was available for ginseng, dried.

tr.td: Metalaxyl (M) and Metalaxyl‐M (MM) are approved in the EU; renewal process for MM was completed in 2020; for M, it is ongoing.
EU TRV available; according to EU assessment, additional tox data required for a number of metabolites. According to JMPR, metabolites are covered by TRV of parent compound.

EU and Codex RD for plants (enforcement) are identical; EU RD for enforcement and RA for animal products contain a common moiety, while the RD derived by JMPR includes specifically parent and specific metabolites and their conjugates. RD for RA of JMPR is wider than EU RD.
Analytical methods for MRL enforcement are available; however, some deficiencies were noted for the method for pineapples.
The proposed Codex MRLs are sufficiently supported by data.
No acute and no chronic intake concern identified.

No critical points for discussion identified. Risk managers to discuss whether the currently ongoing renewal process, including a re‐assessment of the toxicological reference values justifies a general reservation on the proposed Codex MRLs.

caption.p: Comparison of toxicological reference values (TRV) derived by JMPR and at EU level

tr.td:
In the framework of a recent assessment (EFSA, 2023b), it was concluded that due to the deficiencies listed below, the derivation of toxicological reference values according to current scientific standards is not possible and therefore the experts recommended to withdraw the previous EU TRV (previous ADI derived in 2011: 0.015 mg/kg bw per day, previous ARfD derived in 2011: 0.03 mg/kg bw).
According to current standards, the genotoxic potential of bifenthrin was found to be inconclusive.
The assessment of the validity of the toxicological studies and reliability of their results is limited by the lack of details on the toxicological studies reported in the DAR (France, 2005) (e.g. that do not allow to verify the compliance of these studies with the current version of the test guidelines), and the unknown validity of the analytical methods used in feed, body fluids and tissues, air and any additional matrices used in support of the toxicity studies. These limitations imply, for instance, that it is not possible to understand the difference in NOAELs derived by the EU and the JMPR assessments, as is the case of the maternal and developmental toxicity NOAELs of a developmental toxicity study in rats (critical to the risk assessment).
A search for published literature has not been conducted; the JMPR identified a published study (Wolansky et al., 2006) not available to the EU peer review, that was used as the basis to derive an ARfD.
The endocrine disruptive potential of bifenthrin was not assessed according to the current ECHA/EFSA guidance (ECHA and EFSA, 2018). It is expected that additional toxicological information would be needed to perform such an assessment.
An interspecies comparative in vitro metabolism study performed on animal species used in pivotal studies and on human material is not available to determine the relevance of the toxicological animal data to humans and whether additional testing of potential unique human metabolites would be required.

The residues datasets in squash and cucumbers are different (Mann–Whitney H test); thus JMPR decided to use only the residues on summer squash to propose the CXL for cucumbers and summer squash. According to the EU rules at least 8 trials would be needed. Metabolites included in JMPR RD for RA:

A number of metabolite were identified that contain the common moiety 2,2‐difluoro‐benzo[1,3]dioxole‐4‐carboxylic acid. The JMPR concluded that the ADI of fludioxonil applies to metabolites CGA 192155, CGA 339833 and SYN 551031 that contain the common moiety.

Metabolites included in EU RD for RA:
metabolites oxidised to metabolite 2,2‐difluoro‐benzo[1,3]dioxole‐4 carboxylic acid (CGA 192155)

In the previous EU assessment, the applicability of the ADI to metabolites containing the common moiety was not explicitly mentioned. At the time of the peer review, sufficient data was available on metabolite CGA 339833 to conclude in the same line as the JMPR, that the metabolite is covered by the ADI set for the parent. It is expected that in the framework of the renewal process, a more detailed toxicological assessment of metabolites will be provided.

Specific comments: In pecan, results were all below the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg; in almonds, 3 trials were below LOQ; the remaining two trials had residues of 0.018 and 0.15 mg/kg. Only residue trials on almonds were used to derive the Codex MRL proposal because the residue levels were higher than in pecans. In principle, for deriving the group MRL for tree nuts, the combined data of almonds and pecan nuts set should be used. Based on this combined data set, an MRL proposal of 0.2 mg/kg is derived. This MRL would be sufficient to cover the highest observed residues in almonds. IT is noted that the highest result in almonds might be an outlier.
Conclusion: It is recommended to discuss with MS whether the proposed Codex MRL for the group of tree nuts is acceptable, which was derived from the trials in the crop with the highest residues.

caption.p: Summary of the consumer risk assessment

td.p: Not relevant since no ARfD was allocated.

An indicative long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1. The input values of the most recent long‐term risk assessment (EFSA, 2021i) were updated, including the STMR values derived by JMPR for the crops for which the proposed Codex MRL is higher than the EU MRL (i.e. tree nuts, papaya, mango, milk, edible offal).
The calculations are affected by additional, non‐standard uncertainties, related to more comprehensive EU RA‐RD.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ADI.
The calculation is indicative since the RA‐RD for plant derived by JMPR is limited to fludioxonil only.

However, it is noted that the commodities of plant origin for which updated input values were included in the PRIMo calculation (i.e. papaya, mango and tree nuts) belong to the group of fruits and fruiting vegetables, for which a CF of 1 was derived, meaning that the additional metabolites included in the EU residue definition for risk assessment are not expected to occur in significant amounts.

It is noted that JMPR performed a separate exposure calculation for CGA 192155, SYN 551031 and CGA 339833 which are covered by the EU residue definition for risk assessment for plant commodities. Details on this calculation are reported in the last column.
For the metabolites, CGA 192155, SYN 551031 and CGA 339833 which are covered by the TRV of fludioxonil JMPR proposed to use conversion factors to estimate the dietary exposure to combined residues.

For the metabolites CGA 227731, CGA 308565/SYN 518579 (tautomeric pair), CGA 265378, CGA 308103 which are not covered by the TRV of fludioxonil JMPR proposed the TTC approach to demonstrate the level of exposure is unlikely to pose a consumer health concern.
Not relevant
No long‐term consumer health risk was identified.
The overall chronic exposure accounted for 21% of the ADI.
Among the commodities under consideration, milk was identified as the main contributor, accounting for up to 0.65% of the ADI.
Short‐term exposure:
Not relevant (JMPR did not derive an ARfD).
Long‐term exposure:
Max 6% of the JMPR ADI
For CGA 192155, SYN 551031, CGA 339833, JMPR concluded that these metabolites do not contribute significantly to the dietary exposure from fludioxonil.
For fludioxonil uses evaluated by JMPR in 2022 and in previous years, the following exposure was calculated (IEDI):
CGA 308565/SYN 518579: 0.0956 μg/kg bw per day;
CGA 265378 of 0.236 μg/kg bw per day;
CGA 308103 of 0.198 μg/kg bw per day.
For CGA 227731 found only in feed items at insignificant levels, JMPR concluded the dietary exposure is expected to be below 1.5 μg/kg bw per day and is unlikely to pose a public concern.

In the targeted assessment of indoxacarb (EFSA, 2022f), EFSA screened the existing MRLs which are based on CXLs or on import tolerances considering the new toxicological reference values established during the peer review process for the renewal of the approval of indoxacarb and identified the MRLs for which an acute risk could not be excluded and several MRLs that are unlikely to pose a risk for consumers.

Regarding the acute exposure, concerns were identified for 20 existing MRLs derived from CXLs and/or import tolerances (apples, pears, apricots, cherries, peaches, plums, table and wine grapes, tomatoes, peppers, aubergines, cucumbers, gherkins, courgettes, melons, pumpkins, watermelons, broccoli, cauliflower, lettuce) with exposure exceeding up to 2,188% of the ARfD.
The default LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg was found sufficiently protective for the remaining commodities (EFSA, 2022f).

tr.td: Indoxacarb is no longer approved in the EU.
EU TRV available for parent compound. Toxicological profile of metabolites included in the residue definitions for risk assessment not fully addressed.
EU and Codex RDs are comparable, except the RD for RA for processed plant products and for animal products.
Analytical methods for MRL enforcement are available.

The proposed Codex MRLs are sufficiently supported by data. However, due to acute intake concerns, the proposed MRLs for beetroots, milks, bushberries, beans with pods and meat from mammals are not acceptable. A chronic intake concern was identified, if all proposed CXLs are implemented in the EU. Refined calculations excluding the commodities with acute intake concerns might be requested by risk managers.
In the indicative acute risk assessment, intake concerns were identified for a number of commodities.

td.p: Due to intake concerns and other open points related to incomplete toxicological data on metabolites/degradation products to discuss with risk managers the possibility to introduce a reservation.
Considering that the last toxicological assessment of indoxacarb was performed by JMPR in 2005, the substance might be a candidate for being prioritised for periodic review.

Metabolism studies with post‐harvest treatment would be desirable to confirm that no metabolites are formed in significant amounts.

td.p: Metabolites included in JMPR RD for RA: –

JMPR decided not to include the plant metabolite (major metabolite found in potato tuber) in the residue definition; the ADI derived for mandipropamid is not applicable for the metabolite; due to lack of toxicological studies, no separate ADI/ARfD was established. The TTC concept for non‐genotoxic substances was applied for this metabolite.

Metabolites included in EU RD for RA:
SYN 500003 was shown to be more acutely toxic than mandipropamid (oral LD50 1,049 mg/kg bw) and negative in an Ames test; it was not possible to derive reference values for the consumer risk assessment (EFSA, 2012h).

The RMS informed EFSA that the assessment of the metabolite SYN 500003 is subject to the renewal of the active. New data were provided but are not yet assessed (assessment of the tox package of mandipropamid still ongoing and not finalised).

X11719474 (N,N‐[methyl(oxo){1‐[6‐(trifluoromethyl)pyridin‐3‐yl]ethyl}‐λ6‐sulfanylidene]urea)

In the EU assessment (EFSA, 2014d) it was concluded that the ADI for the metabolite is similar to the one established for the parent compound. An additional uncertainty factor (UF) of 2 was applied to the available short‐term toxicity NOAEL for metabolite X11719474 to extrapolate from sub‐chronic to chronic toxicity; an additional UF of 4 was applied to account to the fact that for this metabolite, four isomers exist. Hence the EU peer review experts agreed that the TRVs of the parent shall be applied to the metabolite as well.

If metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for risk assessment will become parent sulfoxaflor only.

The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor.

At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474. X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items.

The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014d). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products was provisional. Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound.

The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

However, as insufficient information was available to perform a combined risk assessment for residues resulting from use with all a.s. which are likely to form these metabolites, JMPR proposed to assess the a.s. separately.

In the EU, a separate enforcement residue definition for plant and animal commodities is set that refers to a soil metabolite difluoroacetic acid (DFA, expressed as DFA). Thus, the EU and JMPR residue definitions are not compatible.

The risk assessment residue definition derived by the JMPR for plant commodities is wider as it includes also 6‐CNA metabolite, which was not proposed to be included in the EU residue definition by the pesticides peer review. Thus, the exposure calculated for this residue definition of JMPR would be overestimated to a certain extent. 6‐CNA is minor metabolite which is a common metabolite with other a.s. (e.g. imidacloprid).
The risk assessment residue definitions for animal commodities set in the EU and by JMPR are comparable.

cGAP: USA, 2 × 0.2 kg a.s./ha, RTI 10 days, PHI 14 days
Number of trials: 8
Sufficiently supported by data: Yes

Specific comments: For deriving the input value for risk assessment, JMPR added the residue found in rotational crop studies (rape seed) assessed by 2016 JMPR to the STMR derived from the primary crop studies. The rotational crop study was performed with an application rate of 2 × 125 g/ha; in the assay with a PBI of 34 days, the residues in rape seed accounted for 0.16 mg/kg. Considering that the critical GAP in view of rotational crops is higher than the tested dose rate, and considering the persistence of soil metabolites (in particular DFA), the study may not be fully representative for the expected residues in sunflowers, resulting from the uptake from soil.

The RMS received an application for an Import Tolerance for flupyradifurone and DFA on sunflower seeds (assessment is ongoing). The trials submitted in support of the import tolerance application for sunflower seed were the same as the ones assessed by JMPR. In line with (EFSA, 2020m) and (EFSA, 2020h), two separate consumer exposure calculation scenarios were performed in order to estimate the exposure to flupyradifurone and DFA residues from (1) animal commodities and treated primary crops and (2) rotational crops. RMS concluded that the combined exposure to flupyradifurone and DFA residues is unlikely to pose a chronic consumer intake concern. The following MRLs were derived to support the US GAP:
Flupyradifurone, expressed as flupyradifurone: 0.8 mg/kg.
DFA, expressed as DFA: 0.06 mg/kg (primary use + rotation).

Conclusion: The proposed Codex MRL (RD parent compound) is acceptable. Further discussion with risk managers is recommended to decide whether the approach taken to derive the risk assessment values (including residues resulting from soil uptake) is acceptable, taking into account the additional information available in the context of an ongoing import tolerance application. In addition, it would be necessary to derive an MRL for the second EU RD, i.e. DFA. According to the RMS assessing the same studies in the context of the import tolerance application, an MRL of 0.06 mg/kg for DFA would be required.
Follow‐up action: To check details in JMPR evaluation and the ongoing import tolerance application whether sufficient information is reported to derive a corresponding MRL for DFA.

In addition, it would be necessary to derive an MRL for the second EU RD, i.e. DFA. According to the RMS assessing the same studies in the context of the import tolerance application, an MRL of 0.9 mg/kg for DFA would be required.

td.p: A short‐term dietary risk assessment (PRIMo rev. 3.1) was performed for the commodities, for which the Codex MRL proposals were derived (i.e. pineapples, sunflower seeds, safflower seeds and sesame seeds).

A long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1. The input values of the most recent long‐term risk assessment (EFSA, 2021d) were updated, including the STMR values derived by JMPR for the crops for which the proposed Codex MRL is higher than the EU MRL (i.e. pineapples, sunflower seeds, safflower seeds and sesame seeds).

It is noted that in (EFSA, 2021d) a separate risk assessment was performed to estimate the residue exposure related to rotational crops. Hence, both exposure calculations were updated by including the input values related to the primary crop use and the residues taken up via soil (rotational crops). However, the rotational crop scenario was updated only for the crops under assessment.

The calculations are affected by additional, non‐standard uncertainties, related to broader residue definition established by JMPR. In addition, residues in rotational crops may be underestimated since the GAP related to the new Codex MRL proposal seems to be more critical than the previously assessed uses in annual crops.

td.p: In 2017, the EU submitted a concern form regarding the residue definition, because quinclorac methyl ester which is 10 times more toxic than quinclorac was not included in the residue definition for enforcement, noting that quinclorac methyl might be used as a variant of the a.s. quinclorac in plant protection products (to be confirmed by the manufacturer of the a.s.).
The EU concern was addressed by JMPR in 2018: JMPR confirmed the previously derived residue definition, highlighting that the overall exposure was low.
The EU reserved its position to include quinclorac methyl ester in the EU residue definition for enforcement for rapeseed, considering the higher toxicity of the methyl ester.

EFSA still has concerns that the RD for enforcement does not cover the more toxic variant quinclorac methyl ester, but acknowledges that the inclusion of a variant for which no data were submitted to JMPR is not in line with the JMPR assessment practice.

The current residue definitions for enforcement established in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 are not directly comparable with the residue definition proposed by JMPR which comprises also the enol‐metabolite. In the framework of the MRL review, the enol‐metabolite was proposed to be included in the residue definition for enforcement, but recommendations of this assessment have not yet been legally implemented.

As regards the risk assessment residue definition (RD‐RA), for plants, JMPR proposed to include not only the enol‐metabolite but also 4‐hydroxymethyl‐Sp‐enol, free and conjugated; the latter was not proposed by the peer review. In the framework of the Article 12 MRL review, two RD‐RA were proposed: (1) primary crops, except leafy crops including spiromesifen‐enol (M01) and (2) for leafy and rotational crops, also including enol (M01), spiromesifen‐4‐hydroxymethyl (M02) and its conjugate M03. It was noted that the inclusion of metabolites M04 and M06 in the residue definition for rotational leafy crops may need to be reconsidered, based on the outcome of a rotational field trial on succeeding leafy (EFSA, 2019a).

Since the proposed Codex MRLs are for fruits and pulses and oilseeds only, for which the RD‐RA is the same in the EU and JMPR, the difference in the RD‐RA derived by JMPR and the EU (for leafy crops and rotational crops) will not have an impact on the assessment.

It is noted that for animal products, residue definitions at the EU level could not be proposed in the absence of appropriate metabolism studies. There are no Codex MRL proposals for livestock commodities.

caption.p: Comparison of toxicological reference values (TRV) derived by JMPR and at EU level

td.p: A different assessment of the data is noted in the derivation of the ADI; the JMPR established an ADI on the basis of a NOAEL of 4.5 mg/kg bw per day for decreased body weight gains in males at 9.2 mg/kg bw per day in a 2‐year toxicity study in rats. This NOAEL was considered a lowest observed adverse effect level (LOAEL) in the EU, and the AU ADI is based on the NOAEL of 0.46 mg/kg bw per day for increased incidence of focal hepatocellular atypia in the 2‐year rat study and applying an UF of 100.

The RMS informed EFSA that in the currently ongoing re‐assessment of fenazaquin, the existing ADI in the EU set at 0.005 mg/kg bw/day and the ARfD of 0.1 mg/kg bw for the parent and the metabolite 4‐hydroxyquinoline (4‐OHQ) are confirmed.

Metabolites included in JMPR RD for RA:
2‐hydroxy‐fenazaquin acid (2,2‐dimethyl‐2‐(4‐(2‐((6‐hydroxy‐4‐quinazolinyl)oxy) ethyl)phenyl)acetic acid)

No data on the toxicity of this metabolite were submitted to JMPR. This metabolite was not detected in rats, but its presence is suggested by oxidative metabolism. JMPR concluded that the toxic effects of the metabolite would be adequately detected in the tests conducted on the parent compound.
4‐hydroxyquinazoline (tautomeric forms of)

JMPR concluded that the ADI and ARfD established for fenazaquin is also applicable to 4‐OHQ (4‐hydoxyquinazoline) and TBPE (tertiary butylphenylethanol), expressed as fenazaquin. However, TBPE was not included in the RD derived by JMPR.

Metabolites considered in EU RD for RA:
2‐(4‐tert‐butylphenyl)ethanol (TBPE):
For the metabolite, separate TRV were established (i.e. ADI 0.002 mg/kg bw per day; ARfD 0.002 mg/kg bw (EFSA, 2013d)).

The RMS informed EFSA that with regard to the metabolite TBPE, the draft renewal assessment suggests that the existing ADI might need to be reduced to 0.0006 mg/kg bw per day, while confirming the ARfD. TBPE is not part of the JMPR residue definition.

td.p: The EU and JMPR enforcement residue definitions for plants are nearly identical, covering only parent fenazaquin. In the EU, for risk assessment, a second residue definition was established for metabolite TBPE. Overall, EU residue definitions for both enforcement and risk assessment for plants are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR derived a global enforcement residue definition. Furthermore, the risk assessment RD for plants derived by JMPR was not used for the risk assessment of pulses and leafy vegetables, as it was derived from metabolism studies in two crop groups (cereals and fruit). Hence requests for setting CXLs for pulses and mint were rejected.

For animals there is a slight difference in the residue definition for enforcement and RA, since EFSA is proposing fenazaquin only (for ruminants), while JMPR proposes a wider RD which includes also metabolites, i.e. tautomeric forms of 4‐hydroxyquinazoline (only for risk assessment) and 2‐hydroxy‐fenazaquin acid (for enforcement and risk assessment).

The RMS informed EFSA that during the renewal of the approval, the residue definitions for plant products (enforcement and risk assessment) are confirmed (still restricted to fruits). The previous tentative residue definition for leafy vegetables is no longer supported by the RMS.
The residue definitions for ruminants are also confirmed during the renewal, but the RMS highlighted that the representative uses do not include feed items and therefore they are not required.

tr.td: No EU peer review and no MRL review

td.p: Plant products: In metabolism studies, parent afidopyropen was the major compound in the majority of primary crop commodities (up to 61% TRR). However, in soya bean, parent afidopyropen was detected at very low concentrations in dry soya bean seed (0.4% TRR, 0.001 mg/kg). The metabolite trigonelline (M031) identified in soya bean seeds (47% TRR) is also a naturally occurring alkaloid in many plants. The dimer M007 was found in dry soya bean seeds at 1% TRR and 12% TRR, depending on the study.

Animal products: Parent afidopyropen was the major compound in animal tissues, ranging from 17% TRR in goat kidney to 97% TRR in egg yolk and up to 6.8% TRR in milk. The ester cleavage metabolite M001 was a major metabolite in milk, liver, kidney and muscle, ranging from 24% to 66% TRR, and was also a minor metabolite in fat (4.6% TRR). M017 was a major metabolite in hen liver. The metabolic pathways in goat and hens are similar to that which is reported in rat.

CPCA is a metabolite that is formed by cleavage of the cyclopropane carboxylic acid ester moieties from the parent molecule. Parent afidopyropen contains two CPCA groups. From livestock and rat metabolism studies it is known that metabolism can lead to the cleavage of only one or both CPCA ester moieties. Including CPCA in the residue definition (expressed as parent compound) seems problematic, since one molecule of afidopyropen may generate 1 or 2 molecules of CPCA. Hence the molecular weight conversion factor to recalculate the amount of CPCA to afidopyropen equivalents could be either 6.9 or 3.45. Hence, this leads to ambiguous results.

In 2021 CCPR, the EU expressed concerns on the appropriateness of the risk assessment residue definitions derived by JMPR, as the inclusion of CPCA in the residue definition for risk assessment may lead to ambiguous results.

According to the results of the livestock metabolism and feeding studies, parent compound was below the LOQ while the levels of the total residues (parent +M001 + CPCA‐carnitine expressed as parent) was more than 20 times higher. Hence, parent compound is considered not a valid marker substance and therefore the RD for enforcement should be reconsidered for muscle/meat and milk.

caption.p: Comparison of toxicological reference values (TRV) derived by JMPR and at EU level

td.p: The ADI and ARfD set by JMPR and at EU level are not comparable.

For deriving the ADI, JMPR selected as point of departure the NOAEL of 20 mg/kg bw per day from the 2‐year study in rats whereas the EU peer review selected the NOAEL of 3.6 mg/kg bw per day from the multi‐generation study. The difference is likely because a different NOAEL for parental toxicity was set by JMPR and EU; adversity regarding the critical effect (increase relative weight) was set at different level by JMPR and EU. JMPR set a higher NOAEL of 26 mg/kg bw per day than in the EU, i.e. 3.6 mg/kg bw per day.

For setting the ARfD, JMPR selected as point of departure the NOAEL of 177 from the acute neurotoxicity study based on clinical signs and mortality at 500 mg/kg bw whereas in the EU the maternal NOAEL of 165 mg/kg bw per day from the developmental rat toxicity study based on mortalities observed at 400 mg/kg bw per day. Although the NOAEL value is the same range, in the EU evaluation, an additional UF of 4 was applied because of the severity of effect (i.e. mortality). An additional UF was not considered justified by JMPR because human exposure is unlikely to result in saturation of renal excretion.

Metabolites included in JMPR RD for RA:
No RD for RA derived. JMPR noted major amounts of unidentified compounds in all matrices investigated in the plant metabolism studies. As these compounds are likely to be present in the harvested commodities for human and for livestock consumption, an identification and further toxicological characterisation was found indispensable.

Consumer health‐based reference values of pyridate were considered applicable to these metabolites.
