caption.p: Summary of the consumer risk assessment

td.p: Not relevant for triflumuron since no ARfD was allocated for triflumuron.

p.bold: RA assumptions (sum of M07 and M08, expressed as M07):

td.p: For soya beans, EFSA calculated an indicative short‐term exposure based on the estimated residue level of M07 derived by JMPR (STMR of 0.02 mg/kg).

The calculation is affected by additional non‐standard uncertainties, because the concentration of M07 were not based on residue trials but was estimated from metabolism studies. M08 was not considered in the JMPR assessment.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ARfD.

p.bold: RA assumptions (sum of triflumuron, M07 and M08):

td.p: A long‐term dietary risk assessment was performed using PRIMo rev. 3.1. The input values of the most recent long‐term risk assessment (EFSA, 2017a) were updated, including the STMR values derived by JMPR for the crops for which the proposed Codex MRL is higher than the EU MRL (i.e. soya bean, mammalian meat/muscle, fat and offal).

The calculations are affected by additional, non‐standard uncertainties, related to the fact that residue levels of metabolites M07 and M08 included in the provisional RD‐RA for pulses and oilseeds are not available nor conversion factors were derived at the EU level.

In addition, it should be highlighted that following the expiry of the EU approval, the lowering of the existing EU MRLs is under preparation since these MRLs were derived exclusively for previously authorised European uses (i.e. in apples, pears, apricots, peaches, plums). As these commodities are still included in the risk assessment, the calculations are likely to overestimate the exposure.
The risk assessment was performed with the EU ADI.

In 2019 the JMPR noted that M02 (free and conjugated) and M07 (free and conjugated) were not analysed in the supervised trials and decided to estimate these concentrations using the following conversion factors derived from metabolism study:
– concentration of M02 (free and conjugate) in soya bean: 2.1 times (0.064 mg eq/kg/0.030 mg eq/kg) higher than parent triflumuron (expressed as triflumuron).

– concentration of M07 (free and conjugated) in soya bean: 2.5 times (0.10 mg eq/kg/0.040 mg eq/kg) higher than parent (expressed as triflumuron). Considering the ratio of molecular weight (191.2/358.7), the concentration of M07 expressed as the compound should be calculated as ×1.4 of triflumuron.
These CFs were used in the consumer risk assessment calculations performed by the JMPR.
An acute risk assessment was performed for metabolite M07.

p.bold: Results for sum of M07 and M08, expressed as M07:

td.p: No short‐term consumer health risk was identified for the crops under assessment.
For metabolite M07 no short‐term acute exposure assessment was identified (max 0.6% of ARfD for soya beans)
No long‐term consumer health risk was identified.
The overall chronic exposure accounted for 22% of the ADI (NL toddler).
Among the crops under consideration, cattle milk was identified as the main contributor, accounting for up to 4% of the ADI.
Long‐term exposure:
The IEDIs ranged from 4% of the JMPR ADI for sum of triflumuron and M02 and 0% of the JMPR ADI for metabolite M07 (17 GEMS/Food consumption cluster diet).
Short‐term exposure:
Metabolite M07
Highest result for: 1% of ARfD (soya bean)

td.p: Peer review (EFSA, 2018g):
1) Mefentrifluconazole
2) TDMs, with a separate assessment of TA and TLA TAA1,2,4‐Triazole
1) Mefentriconazole and metabolite M750F022 and fatty acid conjugates of M750F022, expressed as parent.
2) TDMs, with a separate assessment of TA and TLA TAA 1,2,4‐Triazole

Plant commodities: In the primary crop metabolism studies conducted in grape, soya bean and wheat, mefentrifluconazole was the predominant compound in most of matrices (60–92% TRR) in forage (wheat, soya bean), leaf/stalk (grapevine), straw/hull/chaff (wheat, soya bean), green pod (soya bean) and grape (grapevine). In wheat grain and soya bean seed, mefentrifluconazole was present at very low levels, while TDMs (triazole metabolites, mainly triazole alanine) represented the predominant residues.
In a rotational crop metabolism study in leafy vegetables, root and tuber vegetables and cereals, mefentrifluconazole and TDM were identified as major residues, similar to the primary crops.
The ratio of R‐ and S‐enantiomers of mefentrifluconazole residues in plants remained unchanged compared with the test substance.

The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU level are identical. However, in the EU, additional risk assessment residue definitions comprising the TDMs were set.

Animal commodities: In goat matrices, parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐triazole were the predominant components of the residue. Significant change in the ratio of S:R enantiomers was revealed in most of goat matrices with proportion of the R‐enantiomer of 70–80% in cream, muscle, liver, kidney and fat. A similar shift was observed in liver and kidney of rats.

In poultry matrices, the metabolite M750F022 (and its fatty acid conjugates) is the predominant component of the residue, with parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐T also present as significant components.
Based on this data JMPR proposed the RD for enforcement as mefentrifluconazole (free and conjugated);
At EU level, the residue definition for enforcement only comprises the parent compound (without the conjugates).

EFSA considers the RD for enforcement derived by JMPR not appropriate, because
The individual conjugates are not sufficiently defined; to develop and validate enforcement methods, the individual components need to be available as analytical standards to check if the method is capable to analyse for them (e.g. efficiency of hydrolytic step to convert the conjugate to the unconjugated form).
Currently, no analytical methods are available for enforcement,
The conjugates of the parent compound are of minor relevance;
The parent compound is therefore considered to be an appropriate marker substance.

For risk assessment the JMPR and the EU RD are not comparable, as JMPR also included the conjugates of the parent compound (see discussion of RD for enforcement) and M750F022 (and its conjugates) for all animal products. As the samples of animal products derived in the feeding studies were not analysed for the conjugates, JMPR derived correction factors from the metabolism studies.

caption.p: Summary of available analytical methods

tr.td: Plants (high water, high acid, high fat, dry, other matrices (see remarks))
Extraction with MeOH/H2O; ACN:H2O; Hexane, cleaned up with SPE (QuEChERS) and LC–MS/MS analysis
Method validation data assessed by JMPR 2022 for apple, grapes, citrus, coffee, soya beans, cereals. No validation data available for sugar cane which belongs to high sugar crops group.
Animals (bovine and poultry see the remark)
Extraction with iso‐octane or MeOH/H2O; and LC–MS/MS analysis

Two methods were assessed by JMPR 2022 for the animal commodities (milk, cream, fat, muscle, kidney, liver and eggs). No validation data provided demonstrating that the method is valid to capture the conjugates of parent mefentrifluconazole (which was included in the JMPR residue definition for MRL enforcement).

Sufficient analytical methods are available to enforce mefentriconazole in plant (except sugar cane). For animal matrices, the methods available are validated for the EU enforcement residue definition, but not for the JMPR residue definition.

caption.p: Summary of the assessment

tr.th: Findings relevant for discussion of EU position

tr.td: A.s. approved in the EU. It belongs to the class of triazoles.

For plant products, the enforcement RD set at EU level and by JMPR are identical. For animal products, the enforcement RDs are not compatible. Residue definitions for RA set by JMPR and at EU level are also different, leading to additional uncertainties in the risk assessment.

For plant products, analytical method are available for MRL enforcement, except for sugar cane. For animal products, no validated methods are available for the JMPR assessed by JMPR 2022 do not cover sugar cane (high‐sugar content group).

The proposed Codex MRLs are sufficiently supported by data, except the MRL proposal for tree nuts. Further details still need to be checked in the JMPR evaluation to decide on the acceptability of the MRL proposals for bananas.

An acute intake concern was identified by EFSA and by JMPR for several commodities covered by the Codex MRL proposal for pome fruit, leafy greens, subgroup of and leaves of brassica, subgroup of. Similarly, JMPR noted acute intake concerns for leafy greens and leaves of brassica, subgroup of.
Further discussion at management level is required to derive the EU position.

td.p:
Metabolites included in JMPR RD for RA:
Tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BCS‐CQ63359)
Tetraniliprole‐benzylalcohol (BCS‐CZ91631)
The ADI applies to these metabolites; JMPR also concluded that no ARfD is required for these two metabolites.

JMPR assessed a number of additional metabolites which were not included in the RD for RA.
Tetraniliprole‐desmethyl‐amide (BCS‐CN42374)

Based on its structural similarity to the parent, tetraniliprole‐desmethyl‐amide was predicted to be no more toxic than the parent.
Tetraniliprole‐hydroxy‐N‐methyl (BCS‐CZ91629)
This metabolite was considered to be covered by the parent as it is a major metabolite in the rat.

For a number of metabolites, JMPR concluded that they do not show any alerts for genotoxicity in QSAR analysis. However, they were considered insufficiently similar to the parent to read across their toxicity and hence the Cramer class III threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) of 1.5 μg/kg bw per day should be applied; the following metabolites fall in this category (see below JMPR risk assessment):

td.p: The active substance was never assessed at the EU level – residue definitions have not been proposed at the EU level.

In the plant metabolism studies involving foliar applications (apples, potato, lettuce, paddy rice), soil drench application (tomato), granular in planting hole applications (rice) and seed treatments (potato and maize), in confined rotational crop metabolism studies and in processing studies, tetraniliprole was the major component (apple, tomato, lettuce, tomato, potato) of the radioactive residue. It was noted that apart from one outdoor study in maize and another in potatoes (seed treatment in furrow), all studies were conducted indoor. However, the JMPR concluded that the indoor studies sufficiently cover outdoor uses (since photodegradation was, at the most, only a minor path of degradation of tetraniliprole in soil).
Tetraniliprole is found in all primary crop commodities and is considered suitable as a marker compound. The JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.

Metabolite tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) was the only compound identified in relevant amounts in plant matrices. This metabolite was found at up to 20% TRR in tomato, rice grain and potatoes, but generally at levels ≤ 0.01 mg eq/kg in food commodities. This occurrence was confirmed in the supervised field trials, in which it was only found occasionally above the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg, with tetraniliprole being present at levels about an order of magnitude higher.

Tetraniliprole is not stable under baking/brewing/boiling (pH 5, 100°C, 60 min) and sterilisation (pH 6, 120°C, 20 min) conditions. Under these conditions 65–68% and 1.1–1.5% AR was recovered as parent and 27–30% AR and 94% AR as tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), respectively. Processing under heating indicated conversion of parent tetraniliprole into tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), e.g. mustard greens (up to 20% TRR), broccoli (up to 29% TRR), tomato paste (23–48% TRR) and soya bean meal (up to 81% TRR).

The JMPR concluded that tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) may occur in primary and rotational crops and that the metabolite contributes significantly to the residue in processed commodities. Hence the JMPR agreed to define a residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities as tetraniliprole and tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), expressed as tetraniliprole.

Metabolism in animals was assessed in goat and poultry studies. Tetraniliprole was a major component in all goat tissues (24–71% TRR), poultry fat (26–55% TRR) and eggs (4.2–14% TRR), but it contributes little to the overall residue in poultry muscle (3.7–10% TRR) and liver (1.6–4.2% TRR). Metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was a major compound in eggs and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg) and was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg). Parent tetraniliprole was also the major component in all cattle tissues and milk. Therefore, the JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.

In deciding which compound should be included in the residue definition for dietary risk assessment, the JMPR noted that the tetraniliprole was metabolised into numerous components, of which 17 were accounted for > 10% TRR and/or > 0.01 mg eq/kg.

The metabolites were considered in three categories, either covered by the toxicity of the parent, suitable for assessment by the TTC approach following Cramer Class III or by the TTC approach for genotoxic compounds.

Based on the assessment of metabolites, the JMPR proposed the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for animal commodities as follows: sum of tetraniliprole, tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) and tetraniliprole‐benzylalcohol (BCS‐CZ91631), expressed as tetraniliprole.

EFSA does not fully agree on the residue definition for animal products. In particular, for poultry, parent tetraniliprole seems to be not a good marker substance and therefore the residue definition for enforcement is considered not appropriate.

In addition, tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was found to be a the major compound in eggs (36% TRR, 0.030 mg eq/kg) and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg); it was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg).
In the toxicological evaluation of 2021 JMPR, this metabolite (tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone) was reported to give alerts for genotoxicity using OECD QSAR ToolBox, Version 4.5.
In 2022, JMPR compared the exposure for this metabolite with the TTC Cramer class III threshold (see below JMPR risk assessment).

It is recommended to discuss with MS whether the proposed residue definitions for poultry are acceptable. Further details should also be checked in the JMPR evaluations, e.g. whether new information was available that allows to conclude that metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone does not have genotoxicity alerts.

caption.p: Summary of available analytical methods

tr.td: Extraction with water and acetonitrile, determination by LC–MS/MS
The method is also applicable to measure residues of tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (JMPR 2022)
Two extractions with acetonitrile/water followed by drying and reconstitution in 0.1% aqueous formic acid, determination by LC–MS/MS
The method is also applicable to measure residues of tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone and tetraniliprole‐benzylalcohol (JMPR 2022)

JMPR noted that a modified version of QuEChERS multiresidue (MRM) enforcement method 01463 for determination of tetraniliprole and tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone in plant commodities was a suitable enforcement method, with acceptable recovery rates at relevant fortification levels. This method was validated in tomato, grapes, wheat grain, dry bean seed and rape seed, with an LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg each for both parent and metabolite.

sec.title: Codex MRL proposals
sec.p: A Japanese GAP was reported to JMPR which was supported by five residue trials. However, JMPR concluded that since nostudies on residues in follow‐on and rotational crops were provided, no MRL recommendations were made.

It is noted that at EU level, rice is considered a semi‐permanent crop and usually rotational crop studies would not be required. However, the situation may be different in other rice cultivating regions. See also discussion under General considerations, Section 3.

As regards the residue trials supporting the use in rice, EFSA notes that five trials would not be sufficient, as rice is classified in Codex as a major crop for which a minimum of six to eight residue trials would be required.

td.p: This active substance was never notified and authorised in the EU. No residue definitions are derived at the EU level.

JMPR assessed the metabolism in plants using labelled broflanilide (B‐ring‐U‐14C and C‐ring U‐14C) in the following studies: outdoor with two foliar applications each of 0.025 kg a.s./ha to cabbages, tomatoes and soya beans; two indoor soil applications of 0.40 kg a.s./ha to Japanese radish; applications to flooding water at 0.3 kg a.s./ha followed by a foliar application of 0.15 kg a.s./ha on rice; indoor seed treatment of 10 g a.s./100 kg seeds, eq. to 0.022 kg a.s./ha on wheat; and two outdoor foliar applications of 0.1 kg a.s./ha to tea (JMPR 2022).

In all plant metabolism studies, broflanilide was degraded into DM‐8007 via demethylation or into S(PFPOH)‐8007 via oxidative defluorination (substitution of fluorine with hydroxy group). It was noted that metabolite DM‐8007 was identified in plant metabolism studies as a minor metabolite (< 10% TRR), with levels between 8 to 2500 times lower than the parent. Additionally, this metabolite was analysed in various food and feed commodities from supervised field trials and residues above the LOQ were only detected occasionally, but always at least one order in magnitude lower, compared to parent. Parent broflanilide was the major residue identified component in all matrices, thus broflanilide was considered a good marker for enforcement and for the residue definition for risk assessment in plants (JMPR 2022).

JMPR assessed metabolism studies of broflanilide in lactating goats and laying hens. Lactating goats received labelled broflanilide (B‐ring‐U‐14C and C‐ring U‐14C) orally for 10 consecutive days at 19 ppm (0.62 mg/kg bw per day) and 20 ppm (0.73 mg/kg bw), for the B‐ring and C‐ring respectively. Laying hens received labelled broflanilide (B‐ring‐U‐14C and C‐ring U‐14C) orally for 14 consecutive days at 14 ppm (0.86 mg/kg bw/d) and 15 ppm (0.84 mg/kg bw), for the B‐ring and C‐ring, respectively.

In livestock, parent is not a good marker, since only detected at minor levels in lactating goats' muscle, liver and kidney and eggs white. Metabolite DM‐8007 was detected at very high levels, in both labels, in all livestock tissues, milk and eggs.

In general, the transfer of radioactivity into animal food and feed matrices was low. The metabolism in lactating goats and laying hens is similar, starting with N‐demethylation of parent broflanilide to form the main metabolite DM‐8007, which is either hydroxylated and conjugated, or cleaved to DC‐DM‐8007 (identified using the B‐label) and hippuric acid (identified using the C‐label), via the intermediate benzoic acid. Metabolite DC‐DM‐8007 is subsequently hydroxylated, followed by conjugation.
Based on these results, the JMPR derived the residue definition for enforcement and risk assessment in livestock as sum of broflanilide and metabolite DM‐8007, expressed as broflanilide.

In addition, JMPR concluded that residues of broflanilide are not very persistent under field conditions and does not have the potential to accumulate in soil (JMPR 2022). According to the JMPR, broflanilide is stable under processing.

caption.p: Comparison of toxicological reference values (TRV) derived by JMPR and at EU level

td.p: The JMPR established an ADI of 0.3 mg/kg bw per day based on the NOAEL of 30 mg/kg bw per day for maternal toxicity in a developmental toxicity study in rabbits and offspring toxicity in a 2‐generation reproductive toxicity study in rats and using an UF of 100. The ADI is supported by the NOAEL of 36 mg/kg bw per day from a 1‐year study in dogs.
The ARfD is based on the NOAEL of 125 mg/kg bw for systemic toxicity in a neurotoxicity study in rats and applying an UF of 100.

Metabolites included in JMPR RD for RA:
2‐chloro‐5‐hydroxybenzenesulfonamide (IN‐A5760),
2‐chloro‐5‐methoxybenzenesulfonamide (IN‐F4106)
8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxylic acid (IN‐QEK31)
3‐[[(2‐chloro‐5‐methoxyphenyl)sulfonyl]amino]‐L‐alanine (IN‐QZY47)
8‐chloro‐N‐[(2‐chloro‐5‐hydroxyphenyl)sulfonyl]‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxamide (IN‐REG72)
8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxamide (IN‐RYC33)
3‐[[(2‐chloro‐5‐methoxyphenyl)sulfonyl]amino]‐(2R)‐hydroxypropanoic acid (IN‐TMQ01)
The seven metabolites are considered covered by the TRVs established for the parent.
For additional metabolites (IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TDQ54) which are not covered by the TRV, JMPR calculated the expected exposure and compared it with the Cramer Class III threshold (TTC calculations).
Metabolites included in EU RD for RA: not relevant since at EU level no residue definitions were derived yet.

tr.td: Fluazaindolizine, and free and conjugated forms of the following compounds: 2‐chloro‐5‐hydroxybenzenesulfonamide (IN‐A5760), 2‐chloro‐5‐methoxybenzenesulfonamide (IN‐F4106), 8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxylic acid (IN‐QEK31), 3‐[[(2‐chloro‐5‐methoxyphenyl)sulfonyl]amino]‐L‐alanine (IN‐QZY47), 8‐chloro‐N‐[(2‐chloro‐5‐hydroxyphenyl)sulfonyl]‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxamide (IN‐REG72), 8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxamide (IN‐RYC33) and 3‐[[(2‐chloro‐5‐methoxyphenyl)sulfonyl]amino]‐(2R)‐hydroxypropanoic acid (IN‐TMQ01) (expressed as fluazaindolizine)(a)
No EU peer review and no MRL review

Sum of fluazaindolizine, 2‐chloro‐5‐hydroxybenzenesulfonamide (IN‐A5760), 2‐chloro‐5‐methoxybenzenesulfonamide (IN‐F4106) and 3‐[[(2‐chloro‐5‐methoxyphenyl)sulfonyl]amino]‐(2R)‐hydroxypropanoic acid (IN‐TMQ01) (expressed as fluazaindolizine)
No EU peer review and no MRL review

td.p: (a): This can be implemented by taking the maximum of the sum of compounds containing the imidazopyridine ring and hydrolysed using acid to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) or compounds containing the phenyl ring and hydrolysed to 8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxylic acid (IN‐QEK31) (expressed as fluazaindolizine).

The metabolism of fluazaindolizine applied either as [phenyl‐14C(U)]fluazaindolizine (Ph‐14C) or [imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐5,8a‐14C]fluazaindolizine (IP‐5,8a‐14C) in plants was assessed in the following studies: in tomatoes, indoor, planting seedling into the soil treated by soil drenching at 1.5 kg a.s./ha and 30 days later with a soil direct application at 0.5 kg a.s./ha; in soya beans, seeds sown into soil treated with a drench application at 1 kg a.s./ha; in carrots, seeds sown into treated soil after a soil application of 1.5 kg a.s./ha, and a further application was done 30 days later at 0.5 kg a.s./ha; in potatoes, indoor, seeds sown into treated soil after a soil application of 1.0 kg a.s./ha, a further application was done 30 days later at 1.0 kg a.s./ha; mature sugarcane were transplanted into treated with soil drench application of 1.0 kg a.s./ha (JMPR 2022).

In the confined rotational crop study conducted in a glasshouse, bare sandy loam soil was treated with 14C‐fluazaindolizine at the equivalent of ≈ 1.95 kg a.s./ha (0.9× maximum seasonal rate) and spinach, radish and spring wheat were sown 30, 120 and 300 days after soil application (plant‐back interval, PBI). Fluazaindolizine, IN‐F4106 and IN‐QEK31 were the major residues extracted from soil.

Regarding the residue definition for enforcement in plants, as fluazaindolizine occurs in most crops that have detectable residues a pragmatic option as analysis of other compounds involves an intensive hydrolysis step, the JMPR decided the residue definition for compliance with MRLs in plants should be fluazaindolizine.

Regarding the residue definition for risk assessment for plant commodities the JMPR considered the likely occurrence of the compounds and the toxicological properties of the candidates. Compounds considered were fluazaindolizine, IN‐REG72, IN‐A5760, INF4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54 and their conjugates. Each of the compounds is variously the predominant or a significant residue in primary and rotated crops. The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities should account for residues of fluazaindolizine, and free and conjugated forms of the following compounds: IN‐REG72, IN‐QEK31, IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33 and IN‐TMQ01.

It was noted that the analytical method utilising acid hydrolysis converts conjugates to their free form and also hydrolyses fluazaindolizine to IN‐QEK31 and IN‐F4106, IN‐REG72 to IN‐QEK31 and IN‐A5760 and converts IN‐RYC33 to IN‐QEK31. To avoid double counting when expressing all residues in terms of fluazaindolizine, the JMPR considered the maximum of the sum of IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 or IN‐QEK31 measured after hydrolysis to provide the best measure of the compounds included in the residue definition.

To derive the input values according to the residue definition for dietary risk assessment proposed for plant commodities, JMPR added to the residue concentration of parent compound the maximum concentration of either the sum of compounds containing the imidazopyridine ring and hydrolysed using acid to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) or the compounds containing the phenyl ring and hydrolysed to IN‐QEK31 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) were used. The information provided in the JMPR report however is not sufficiently detailed to provide comments whether the approach used by JMPR and the derived risk assessment values are appropriate.

In addition, a field rotational crop study was assessed by the JMPR, and it was concluded that, at the maximum use pattern considered by the JMPR, soil application at up to 2.24 kg a.s./ha, residues of fluazaindolizine and metabolites are expected in rotational crops.

JMPR assessed studies on the metabolism of fluazaindolizine labelled on [Ph‐14C(U)]‐fluazaindolizine and [imidazo‐(1,2‐α)‐pyridine‐2‐14C]‐fluazaindolizine in lactating goats and laying hens and separate studies following dosing with metabolites IN‐QEK31 (lactating goats, laying hens) and IN‐QZY47 (lactating goats) and IN‐TMQ01 (lactating goats).

Regarding the residue definition for enforcement for animal commodities, fluazaindolizine was present in milk, eggs and all tissues in the lactating goat and most tissues in laying hen metabolism studies and would be suitable for monitoring compliance. Thus, the JMPR decided the residue definition for compliance with MRLs in livestock should be fluazaindolizine.

In deciding which compounds should be included in the residue definition for risk assessment for animal commodities, JMPR considered the likely occurrence of the compounds and the toxicological properties of the candidates. The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for risk assessment for animal commodities should be the sum of fluazaindolizine, IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine).

The residue definition for enforcement derived by the JMPR is the same as the residue definition in the EU (by default, parent only). Since the substance was never assessed in the EU there is no RD‐RA established at the EU level.
Overall, based on the information provided in the JMPR report, EFSA would tend to disagree on the proposed residue definitions:
As regards the residue definition for plants (MRL enforcement), the parent compound is considered not an appropriate marker substance, since parent compound was only a minor component of the residue.

In animal products, the livestock metabolism studies showed that parent compound is transferred to animal matrices; however, considering that parent compound is only a minor component of the residues in feed, it might not be a relevant marker compound for MRL enforcement in animal matrices.

The residue definition for animal matrices relevant for risk assessment should also better reflect the expected residues resulting from the intake of fluazaindolizine related residues (metabolites in feed items).

For the risk assessment residue definition (plant matrices), JMPR proposed a new approach, including metabolites and/or hydrolysis products generated under the drastic conditions applied in the analytical methods used to analyse the samples, where degradation products of both ring systems were produced. To derive the risk assessment values, the maximum of the two groups of metabolites containing either the benzene‐ring or the imidazo‐pyridine‐ring system should be taken into account.

Since there is only limited experience on this approach, EFSA would need to verify the details of the assessment. Hence, it is proposed to await the publication of the JMPR evaluation, to perform a more detailed assessment and conclude on the appropriateness of the residue definitions proposed by JMPR.
As the assessment of this substance is ongoing at EU level, proposals for EU residue definitions are expected to be presented by the RMS which will be further discussed by MS experts in due course.

tr.td: Extraction with methanol/water (for high‐oil content matrices, additional step to partition against hexane and discard hexane phase). Determination with LC–MS/MS
Yes, but results are not reported in detail.

td.p: This method is considered suitable for MRL enforcement (RD parent compound). In addition, this method allows determination of the following metabolites: free IN‐F4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐R2W56, IN‐REG72, IN‐TEQ01, IN‐RYC33.
In the residue trials, the samples were subject to additional analysis involving a hydrolysis step to determine the hydrolysed metabolites (see below).

tr.td: Extraction with methanol/water, hydrolysis of extracts with concentrated HCL at elevated temperature, clean‐up and determination with LC–MS/MS
Yes, but results are not reported in detail.

td.p: To measure compounds hydrolysed to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54.
In the hydrolysis step, fluazaindolizine is converted to IN‐F4106, and IN‐QEK31, IN‐REG72 to IN‐A5760 and IN‐QEK31 and IN‐RYC33 to IN‐QEK31.

tr.td: Extraction with acetonitrile/water, determination with LC–MS/MS
Yes, but results are not reported in detail.
Determination of fluazaindolizine and its metabolites (free IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐REG72, IN‐QEK31, IN‐R2W56 and IN‐RYC33).

td.p: The methods for plants involve two parts. Part 1: analysis without hydrolysis (fluazaindolizine and free IN‐F4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐R2W56, IN‐REG72, IN‐TEQ01, IN‐RYC33); Part 2: with hydrolysis of compounds to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12, IN‐TQD54. Hydrolysis of fluazaindolizine and IN‐REG72 results in cleavage of the amide bond and formation of INF4106 plus IN‐QEK31 and IN‐A5760 plus IN‐QEK31.

Residues are reported in terms of analytes but may be converted to parent equivalents using molecular weight conversion factors: 2.26 for IN‐A5760, 2.11 for IN‐F4106, 1.77 for IN‐QEK31, 1.52 for IN‐QZY47, 1.51 for IN‐TMQ01, 1.59 for IN‐UJV12 and 1.58 for IN‐TQD54.
The JMPR concluded that sufficiently validated methods are suitable to measure fluazaindolizine and its metabolites in plants and livestock commodities.

As only limited information is provided in the JMPR report and the substance has not yet been assessed at EU level, EFSA suggests to assess the appropriateness of the methods for enforcement in more detail, once the JMPR evaluation is published.

td.p: For primary crop uses, JMPR reported the results for the parent compound measured in the individual residue trials. In addition, the results for the total residues for dietary risk assessment were reported. However, the level of detail reported in the JMPR report does not allow to verify the non‐standard approach used for the calculation of the risk assessment values. Furthermore, residues were reported for metabolites for which exposure calculations were performed (metabolites IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54) and exposure compared to TTC thresholds. For feed items, residues of IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106 and IN‐TMQ01, IN‐QZY47, IN‐F4106 and INA5760 were retrieved to be used in the livestock dietary burden calculations.

Rotational crop studies: It is also noted that only limited information was reported in the JMPR report on the fate and behaviour of the a.s. in the environment, in particular on soil degradation (DT50, degradation kinetic of a.s. and metabolites in soil, estimation of plateau concentrations etc). Hence, EFSA cannot provide detailed comments whether the approach used by JMPR to derive the MRL proposals for annual crops is in line with the EU approach.
Field rotational crop studies were used to derive estimates of residues in various crop groups. Where necessary, results were scaled to the critical GAP.

When there were multiple crops within a rotational crop category (e.g. leafy vegetables, where residue data were available for lettuce, spinach, radish tops, turnip tops and Swiss chard), the highest of the STMR/median residues and HR/highest residues for the individual crops were selected for the STMR/median and HR/highest residue for the crop grouping. The detailed results are not reported in the JMPR report to verify the appropriateness of the non‐standard approach used to derive MRL proposals.

Similar to primary crop uses, JMPR derived the residue concentrations for the TTC calculation for metabolites IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54 from rotational crop studies. In addition, for livestock dietary burden calculation, residues of IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106 and IN‐TMQ01, IN‐QZY47, IN‐F4106 and INA5760 were also retrieved from the rotational crop studies. Where necessary, processing factors were derived to estimate the residue concentrations in by‐products used for feed purpose.
Further risk management discussions are therefore required to deicde on the acceptability of the MRL proposals.

MRL proposals for animal products: JMPR calculated the dietary burden of livestock considering the results of primary crops and rotational crops used for feed purpose. The DB calculations were performed for parent and for metabolites/group of metabolites included in the risk assessment residue definition for livestock and for the compounds for which the TTC approach was used (IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54). In some of the DB calculations, the EU livestock exposure was the highest compared to other livestock diets. A more general discussion is recommended with MS to agree on a position for MRL proposals for animal products which are based on a EU dietary burden calculation, although the a.s. is not approved in the EU.

Feeding studies were available for parent compound and for metabolite IN‐QEK31, which was a major metabolite in feed items. In addition, metabolism studies were used to estimate the residue concentration for some metabolites.

To derive the MRL proposals and the risk assessment values for animal commodities, the results of the different calculations were combined. From the data presented in the JMPR report, the appropriateness of the non‐standard approach used by JMPR could not be confirmed.

Processed products: Standard hydrolysis studies investigating the degradation under conditions representative for pasteurisation, boiling and sterilisation were not reported in the JMPR report. Processing factors were derived for fluazaindolizine. JMPR also derived processing factors for metabolites [IN‐F4106 + 1.068 × IN‐A5760], IN‐QZY47, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54, used as inputs to calculate total residues and for estimation of livestock dietary burden. The information presented in the JMPR report is not sufficient to assess whether the non‐standard approach used to derive the processing factors is appropriate. Currently no EU MRLs are established for processed products.

tr.td: EU MRL applications or other EU assessments

The RMS has performed an ED assessment in the context of the EU approval procedure (which has been withdrawn in the meantime) and concluded that fluindapyr caused adverse reproductive, parental and offspring effects of human relevance. According to the RMS, ED criteria for EATS modalities are met. US EPA also came to the conclusion that fluindapyr induced substantial adverse reproductive, offspring and parental effects.

No EU peer review and no MRL review

td.p: The JMPR assessed metabolism studies in plants with phenyl‐14C and pyrazole‐14C labelled fluindapyr; the studies were performed with foliar applications in four different crops.

The enantiomeric ratio R:S in some crops remained 50:50 (grape leaves and rinse, sugar beet foliage), however, in other crops a shift could be observed into a ratio ranging from 60:40 to 70:30 (grape, wheat forage/hay/straw, rice grain/straw, soya bean hay/forage).

The metabolic pathways of fluindapyr where similar in the crops investigated, mainly through hydroxylation and oxidative‐N‐demethylation, both followed by conjugation. Parent fluindapyr was a major residue in grapes, sugar beet root, wheat grain and rice grain. Major identified metabolites were 1‐OH‐Met‐fluindapyr (free and conjugated), 3‐OH‐fluindapyr, 1‐OH‐Met‐N‐DesMet‐fluindapyr (free and conjugated) in soya bean forage only and DesMet‐fluindapyr‐conjugates in soya bean forage and hay only.

Metabolism studies in lactating goats and laying hens showed that metabolism proceeds mainly by demthylation to N‐DesMet‐fluindapyr and hydroxylation to 1‐OHMet‐fluindapyr, with further sulphation being (mainly in hen tissues) and glucuronidation (goat tissues).
Hydroxylation leading to 3‐OH and 5‐OH species in hens and di‐OH‐fluindapyr species in goats was also observed.

Fluindapyr is the major component found in the majority of the goat and hen tissues and 1‐OH‐Met‐fluindapyr was a major metabolite in tissues. Other metabolites include 1‐COOH‐fluindapyr (goat liver and kidney and hen liver and muscle), N‐DesMet‐fluindapyr in hen liver only, 1‐OH‐Met‐N‐DesMet‐fluindapyr and its glucuronides in goat kidney, and 1‐SO4‐Met‐fluidapyr in hen liver.

tr.td: Extraction with acetonitrile/water, direct analysis with LC–MS/MS.
Method is also applicable for the determination of 3‐OH‐fluindapyr, 3‐OH‐fluindapyr and DesMet‐N‐fluindapyr‐glycoside.

Extraction with acetonitrile (except fat and milk), followed by extraction with acetone/water; for milk extraction with acetonitrile; for fat, extraction with acetonitrile/hexane. Determination with analysis with LC–MS/MS.
Radio validation demonstrated that method is not appropriate for the determination of parent fluindapyr in milk, muscle, liver, eggs and fat as the recovery was max. 28%.

td.p: An analytical method for the analysis of plant matrices is available.
No suitable analytical method exists to measure fluindapyr in animal commodities.

td.p: Inpyrfluxam and 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 (free or conjugated) expressed as inpyrfluxam

tr.td: No EU peer review and no MRL review

td.p: The default residue definition for enforcement is parent only, which is same RD for enforcement derived by the JMPR.

The JMPR assessed plant metabolism studies performed with either [pyrazolyl‐14C] or [phenyl‐14C] labelled inpyrfluxam (JMPR 2022). Plant metabolism studies were conducted in apple and soya bean (foliar spray), rice (foliar and granular treatments) and maize, sorghum rapeseed and potato (seed treatment) at rates that accommodate the anticipated maximum total seasonal GAP application rates. The JMPR concluded that the metabolism was similar in all crops. The metabolism in rotational crops was similar to the metabolism observed in primary crops and the processing of inpyrfluxam is not expected to modify the nature of residues.

Inpyrfluxam was the predominant residue in apple (up to 79% TRR; 0.24 mg/kg), mature rice grain (up to 78.6% TRR; 0.039 mg /kg) and potato tubers (up to 15% TRR; 0.002 mg/kg) but was only found at very low concentrations in mature soya seed (up to 2% TRR; < 0.001 mg/kg). In feed commodities, parent was detected in soya bean forage (up to 50.5% TRR; 0.79 mg /kg), soya bean hay (up to 22.1% TRR; 0.5 mg/kg), immature pods (up to 65.2% TRR; 0.41 mg/kg), rice straw (up to 77.8% TRR; 0.72 mg/kg) and rice hulls (up to 52.5% TRR; 0.88 mg/kg). In the confined rotational crops study, parent was detected in mature lettuce (up to 26.9%; 0.027 mg/kg) and radish immature and mature roots (up to 58.9%; 0.045 mg/kg) at 30 to 365 days PBI.

The JMPR derived a residue definition for enforcement as parent inpyrfluxam only. Following consideration of the occurrence in plants and the toxicity of several metabolites, the JMPR decided that the residue definition for risk assessment should be inpyrfluxam only.

The metabolic fate of inpyrfluxam was investigated in lactating goats using [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and [phenyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam for five consecutive days at 0.51 mg/kg body weight/day (13.74 ppm feed per day) for [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and at 0.64 mg/kg body weight/day (15.74 ppm feed per day) for the [phenyl‐14C]inpyrfluxam and in laying hens using [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and [phenyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam for seven consecutive days at 12.44 ppm feed per day for [pyrazolyl‐14C] inpyrfluxam and at 13.13 ppm feed per day for the [phenyl‐14C]inpyrfluxam.

In animal metabolism studies, inpyrfluxam was observed in poultry fat (up to 81% TRR; 0.075 mg eq/kg), goat fat (up to 15.8% TRR; 0.004 mg eq/kg) and eggs (up to 11% TRR; 0.002 mg eq/kg). In the feeding studies, parent was only present at 0.017 mg/kg in poultry fat from the highest dose group but not in any other animal tissue, milk or egg. Besides parent inpyrfluxam, metabolite 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 (free or conjugated) was a major residue in most animal matrices and the predominant residue found in the livestock feeding studies.
Parent and metabolite 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 residues were predominantly found in liver and kidney commodities.

In goats, concentrations between fat and muscle were close to the LOQ without clear tendency for accumulation in the fat. In poultry metabolism studies, fat contained approximately 30× higher residue concentrations compared to muscle. However, no accumulation was observed in milk fat or egg yolk. In the feeding studies, residues were generally low, not allowing estimation of ratios between fatty and non‐fatty tissues. The JMPR decided that the residue is not fat‐soluble.

The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for compliance with the MRL and dietary risk assessment for animal commodities should be: inpyrfluxam and 1′‐CH2OH‐S‐2840 (free or conjugated) expressed as inpyrfluxam.
At EU level residue definitions for risk assessment are not established for plants and animals since the substance was not yet evaluated in the EU.

The data set for the EAS‐modalities was considered as sufficiently investigated with no evidence of adversity (scenario 1a). Therefore, for the EAS‐modalities, the ED criteria for humans according to point 3.6.5 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, as amended by Commission Regulation (EU) 2018/605, were considered not met.

However, the assessment of the endocrine disruption properties of isoflucypram for humans for the T‐modality could not be finalised. Further assessment is needed on the impact of the observed changes in the thyroid on the most sensitive population of concern for thyroid toxicity (dams, fetuses and newborns) (EFSA, 2022d).

td.p: At EU level, the same metabolism studies (primary crops, rotational crops and livestock) were assessed as by JMPR.
Overall, EFSA proposed parent isoflucypram as the residue definition for MRL enforcement for plant and animal products.

The risk assessment, residue definitions for animal products is provisional; the residue definition for risk assessment for plant products is limited to cereals only (EFSA, 2022d). The same residue definition as in primary crops was proposed provisionally also for rotational and processed commodities.

JMPR proposed only a residue definition for enforcement as isoflucypram for plant and animal products. For risk assessment, JMPR could not derive a conclusion on the residue definition due to the lack of genotoxicity studies for two metabolites found in rotational crop studies exceeding 0.01 mg eq./kg in mature Swiss chard (i.e. M52 and M54). The dietary exposure for these two metabolites was above the TTC for compound with potential genotoxicity.

Primary crops: Metabolism studies in tomatoes, wheat, soya bean and rapeseed following foliar application and on root potatoes following the postharvest treatment. Isoflucypram was the major compound in all edible parts of the crops (max 93% TRR in wheat grain, 98% TRR in tomato fruits, etc) and in cereals feed items (up to 63% TRR in straw and 55% TRR in hay). Other relevant compounds found in relative and/or absolute amount were: M01 (isoflucypram‐propanol) and M06 (isoflucypram desmethyl propanol) free and conjugates in wheat straw and hay, in soya bean forage and hay were found also the M44 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐homo GSM), M45 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐Cys‐MA), M46 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐OH), M47 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐Glyc), M48 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid – propil‐OH‐Glyc) and M58 (isoflucypram‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide) in potato tuber.
M01 and M06 free and conjugates were found in residue trials on cereals (i.e grains) at levels either comparable or higher than the parent.

Based on metabolism studies and field trials the residue definition for risk assessment at EU level was proposed as: sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and conjugates expressed as isoflucypram limited to cereals only. For enforcement the residue definition was proposed as isoflucypram.

JMPR considered M01 could be excluded from the risk assessment based on the results from residue trials, due to the low occurrence of quantifiable residues in cereals; M06 was assess by using the TTC approach (Cramer Class III) and was found not relevant for risk assessment by JMPR.

In rotational crops, several compounds such as M49 (BCS‐CR60082), M52 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐Cys) and M54 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐GSH) occurred above 10% of TRRs, different than in primary crops. Isoflucypram was found only in wheat forage. For the metabolites M52 and M54, a potential concern for genotoxicity was identified at EU level. JMPR applied the TTC approach to assess M52 and M54, and concluded that the exposure was above the threshold for genotoxic compounds (0.0025 μg/kg bw per day).

Processing studies: Under standard hydrolysis conditions of pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation submitted during peer review isoflucypram and M01 are stable (98%). M06 degraded into M77 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol‐aldehyde) under boiling/brewing/baking up to 66% and under sterilisation up to 98%). Since for M77 a genotoxicity potential could not be excluded, in the EU peer review process, a data gap was set to address genotoxicity, since the precursor substance M06 was found in barley grain at relevant levels.

Animal metabolism studies: Isoflucypram was found in all animal tissues, in milk and eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were recovered at relevant amount in almost all matrices, except M01 in milk and ruminant fat. M07 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐1,2 propandiol), M11 ((isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐carboxylic acid) and M12 isoflucypram‐carboxylic acid) were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver. However, based on poultry feeding studies M07, these metabolites were not expected above 0.01 mg/kg. In ruminants, additional compound such as M02 (isoflucypram‐2 propanol), M19 (conjugate of M01), M20 (conjugate of M02) and M50 were found as relevant; in the EU assessment, for M50 (isoflucypram‐N‐methyl‐pyrazole carboxylic acid) the genotoxicity potential was considered not addressed.

JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of cereal grain processing data for isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol (M06)
Hydrolysis of the extracts from soya bean metabolism studies
In the EU assessment, potential concerns for genotoxicity based on positive genotoxicity QSAR predictions were identified (M50, M66, M67, M77).

caption.p: Summary of available analytical methods

tr.td: Plants (high water, high acid, high oil, high starch/and or protein, dry (straw) matrices (see remarks))

td.p: Several methods were considered validated by JMPR to analyse isoflucypram and the metabolites as following:
– Method 01457‐isoflucypram and M49;
– Methods LN‐002‐P16‐01 and 01520 analysing for isoflucypram only;
– Method 01564 analysing for isoflucypram, M01 and M06 (free and conjugates) in wheat green material, grain and straw.
Analytical method is able to analyse: isoflucypram, M01, M02, M06, M11 and M12.
JMPR consider the method as fully validated.
0.01 (plants)
0.005 (animal)
Analytical method is able to analyse isoflucypram in high water, high oil and animal matrices but not suitable for high starch, cereals and oilseed animal feeds.
JMPR consider the method as fully validated.
According to JMPR the methods available are fully validated and suitable to analyse all isoflucypram and the metabolites M01, M06 (free and conjugates) and M49.
At EU level sufficient method are available to enforce isoflucypram.

sec.title: Codex MRL proposals
sec.p: Not relevant. No assessment of residue data.

sec.title: Consumer risk assessment
sec.p: Not relevant. No assessment of residue data.

caption.p: Summary of the assessment

tr.th: Findings relevant for discussion of EU position

tr.td: The assessment of the a.s. for approval in the EU is ongoing.

td.p: EU TRV available.
In the EU assessment, data gaps were identified to address the genotoxic potential of some metabolites (i.e. M50, M67, M66, M77).
JMPR also identified data gaps for two metabolites (M52 and M54).
The EU and JMPR RDs proposed for MRL enforcement are identical.

For risk assessment, JMPR did not derive residue definitions, because data on genotoxic potential was not available for two metabolites M52 and M54 (exposure was calculated to exceed TTC threshold for genotoxic substances).

In addition, JMPR noted that additional information would be desirable to derive proposals for residue definitions for plant and animal products, such as processing studies for cereal grain for isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol (M06) and information on the hydrolysis of the extracts from soya bean metabolism studies.
At EU level, a EU residue definition was proposed in the EFSA conclusion for plant products (for foliar use in cereals). For animal products, the residue definition was provisional.

tr.td: Several analytical methods were provided in the JMPR report for plant and animal commodities capable to analyse isoflucypram, M01, M06 free and conjugates and M49. Validation data were not reported in detail.
No Codex MRL proposal under assessment.
To discuss with Member States the EU position, considering that a final EU decision on the approval of isoflucypram has not yet been taken.
